speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), the House went into committee on Bill No. Ill, to enable Canadians on active military service during the present war to exercise their electoral franchise; Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
On section 1-soldiers entitled to vote:

It was suggested by the Prime Minister that all British subjects who are enlisted in the Canadian forces should be entitled to vote, whether or not they have attained the age of 21 years. I suggest that this section be amended by striking out the words "of 21 years of age or upwards" after the word "subject" in the first line. All those who have enlisted are doing men's work, and I think that they should be entitled to vote.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As the lion.
member knows, this Bill did not come down originally as a Government measure, but was reported by a committee to whom certain of the laws relating to elections were referred for amendment. Conse-iquently, the Bill has not received the consideration of the members of the Government as a whole which such measures usually do receive. I expressed an opin-tion which has just been made by my hon. friend, and I am still of that opinion.
I 3hall be glad if the section is allowed to stand until the afternoon, in order that it may receive a little further consideration at our hands. I think there is a great deal of force in the hon. member's suggestion,
It seems to me that this provision does not adequately define where the soldier shall vote.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: You mean where his vote shall be counted?

Yes. I think that should be made considerably more definite than it is. As I read the section, it would seem practically to permit the soldier qualified to vote in two places to vote in whichever place he chose. I am aware that the section does not say that, tout I do not see how he is prevented from making whatever choice he pleases. I would toe very much better satisfied' if the section said the soldier should vote in the place where he resided for thirty days toefore his enrollment, and let that toe his definite qualification. Then we would know where we were at; tout toy the proviso the qualification is shifted from one leg to the other, and it is a most undesirable situation in which to find the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It seems to me that the proviso makes it perfectly cleaT that if a man, irrespective of 'being a soldier, is a qualified voter in any particular electoral district, he shall vote in that electoral district only. He does not have a choice; he is, under the proviso, to vote in the elec-

toral district in which he is qualified'. It seemed to us in the drafting of the Bill that, as far as possible, we ought to leave things in the constituency in their normal situation and interfere with the normal situation only to such extent as might toe absolutely necessary in order to carry out the provision that gives every soldier a vote. Under the clause as it stands the soldier who is a qualified voter in any particular electoral district remains a qualified voter in that particular electoral district just as though this Act had not been passed, and all that he gets out of this Act is the method furnished to him toy which he can exercise that right. It seemed to us more proper that the man who is a voter in a particular electoral district ought not to be allowed to transfer himself to another electoral district. If, as the hon. member suggests, you make it imperative that all soldiers shall vote in the places in which they resided 30 days before enlistment, you make a situation where, in some particular place, where enlistmetnt was carried on upon a large scale, you will have transferred into that electoral district from a number of other electoral districts a very large number of votes which may, under conceivable circumstances, override the vote of the ordinary voters in that district; and, on the other hand, you may take out of the electoral district to which each of these soldiers as voters belonged' under the general law, a very large number of persons entitled to vote in that district. The' effect of doing these two things might be to entirely modify the complexion of one or more constituencies. As far as it was possible to do so consistently with giving the soldiers a vote, we sought not to disturb the conditions in the different constituencies; and, notwithstanding what the hon. gentleman has pointed out, it seems to me that the policy of the section, if I may use that term, is very much preferable to a system that would make this law operate to take all soldiers who are actual voters in a particular electoral district forcibly out of that district and transfer them to some other district where they might happen to have been residing before enrollment. The clause as it stands, with the proviso, seemed to us to so operate as to cause the least possible disturbance .of existing conditions, and that seems to me to be a very desirable thing.

It seems that the Minister of Justice has just now struck the crux of this situation which makes it bad. All his suggestions imply that an election is to

be held on the voters1 list as it is at present constituted. But supposing an election is held, not this year, but on the voters' list which is prepared this year, what does he [DOT] say about these absentees from each electoral district who may be on the voters' list now. but who, when the lists are revised this coming summer, will be struck off in consequence of their absence? Do these parties remain on the voters' list because they are soldiers abroad? The Bill does not provide for that. If the Bill provides that because a man may be nonresident in a district through being abroad on war service he is to be considered an elector in that electoral district, you may then possibly overcome this difficulty; but these votes will be counted on the evening of polling day, after the other votes throughout the whole electoral district are counted.

They would all
be counted at the same time, after the poll closes.

They cannot all be
counted at the same time because the Bill provides that the returning officer is to fix a time after the poll is closed to count the vote. Every one knows that the vote is counted in each electoral polling subdivision as soon as the poll is closed. The return is immediately and as quickly as possible sent to the county town or wherever the central office happens to be. These returns would show that one candidate was elected by a small majority. As I suggested last night, here is where one of the difficulties will come in.

The hon. gentleman misunderstands the Bill. Supposing there are twenty polls in an electoral district. Then the counting of the soldiers' ballots by the returning officer makes the twenty-first poll, and the return from it will come as quickly as the others, the returning officer himself being the person who counts the soldiers' ballots and not the deputies.

I may not have the superabundant ability of the hon. member for Calgary, but I think I understand this Bill and I feel very confident I understand the effect it will have. When the vote is polled the candidates or their representatives can be present and see the vote counted. When the returning officer opens the envelopes to count the votes, he sees the name of some man. What does he do? He must look over the voters' list to see whether or not that man is on the list and entitled to vote

in that district. He does not find his name on the voters' list; his name need not be on the list if he swears he is a resident. How do you know whether he is a resident there or not? There is where the great difficulty and uncertainty will come, and that is the very point that will create all the dissatisfaction in the event of the soldiers' vote changing the result of the poll in that particular locality.
That is my objection to this Bill. Of course, if an election were held on the present voters' list the difficulty would be overcome to some extent. I shall be very sorry if the Government do have an election this year-and it looks as if that is what they intend-but it will certainly overcome part of the difficulty. But, if the election is not held this year, the name of every soldier on the voters' list now for any particular district will be struck off, unless there is a clause in the Bill providing that their residence shall be assumed on account of their being away as soldiers.

I wish to follow the remarks of the Minister of Justice. While his statement of the intent of the section is, of course, to be accepted as a pious declaration, there are no means of insisting that that intent shall be carried out. The volunteer signs a declaration that he has not cast any other ballot paper, but there is nothing to show the elector in Saskatchewan or Alberta, where we have no voters' lists, whether he is qualified or not to vote in any particular locality. He could claim qualification to vote in a certain locality where he is not entitled to cast his vote, and he might do that quite conscientiously. If this is to be a legitimate attempt to count the soldiers' vote the way he gave it, there should be a definite knowledge as to where the soldier is entitled to vote, and his vote should be confined to that locality. I quite appreciate what my hon. friend said about the undesirability of unhinging the voting representation of an electoral district; but it is far better that the representation should be unhinged, and Chat we should know definitely what the rights of the voters are and with whom we have to deal, than that it should be unhinged just the same, and nobody should know the limitations of their rights, or how they can keep those rights within those limitations. If we have to go up against a proposition like this, in all conscience let us know exactly what we are going up against. Do not let it be a case of thimble and pea- maybe it is here, and maybe it is not.

I think I can make clear that provision has been made to meet the objection raised by my hon. friend; for I also was impressed with the necessity of making such a provision. This section was drawn with the intention of providing for two classes: it provided, first, that those who resided in the locality for thirty days prior to enlisting should have a vote in that locality; and, secondly, that those wh* had been continuously resident in some locality before they enlisted, should have their votes where they had always had them. I think that is what my hon. friend desires.
I am not urging one way or the other; but I say it should be one way or the other.

My hon. friend will pardon me for saying that that is what he desired, for he does not desire anything. The affidavit as drawn did not make clear the distinction to which he has directed attention. I happened to be out of the city when the Bill was finally drawn, but I have since submitted an alternative to the affidavit on page 6, by which it will be made clear that if the soldier has resided in a community for a longer period than thirty days his vote will be counted at that place where he would have exercised his franchise had be been home. Let me take a concrete case. One of the electors in West Calgary, we will say, is voting under this Act. He will vote in West Calgary. But if he happened to enlist in Edmonton, and had resided in Edmonton for thirty days prior to enlistment, his vote would be counted in Edmonton. I am quite as anxious as my hon. friend to meet the objection he has raised; and, as I have said, we are adding a paragraph to that affidavit which will meet that objection. I realized that one could not ask for a specific provision for our two provinces, but that such a provision should be inserted in the affidavits as would allow a residence vote to be counted in the constituency in which the soldier has lived, unless his residence at the point of enlistment qualified him for a vote at that place only. Have I made myself clear?
Yes, but the fact still remains that there is no possible means of checking the right of a man to vote in one place or the other.

We are introducing this affidavit into the Bill so that when the clerk of the Crown in Chancery looks at the envelope in the first instance, he will be able to allocate the votes to West Calgary
or East Calgary or West Edmonton or East Edmonton as the case may be.
How will he know?

On the back of the envelope there will be certain information to enable him to do that. When the affidavit is finally checked by the returning officer, in the presence of scrutineers of both parties, and it appears that a ballot has been improperly allotted to Edmonton, then of course it will be rejected and returned to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. The very difficulty that my hon. friend has mentioned was anticipated by the committee, and dealt with in the manner I have indicated.
How does the envelope or affidavit show to what constituency the vote should go?

The voter has to make
in the affidavit a distinct statement of what his residence had been for the thirty days prior to enlisting, and also if he had only resided there for thirty days. He will have to say:	For thirty days prior to
enlisting I resided at such and such a place. And if it is a longer period than thirty days, he will have to say, for instance: I resided at 1210 Sixteenth street, Edmonton. Then it will be aparent that he resided in West Edmonton, and should vote there.
-Take people who are close to the line between two post offices.

That was traversed in
the committee, and it was felt that in such a case there might be a mistake in the ballots. In some cases men have lost their votes under the existing law. But this is not the average case.

I was speaking about
the definiteness of the information. There wdll be a multitude of people who have to come fifteen or twenty miles to a post office, and who do not know what riding they are in.

It was felt that on the
instructions there should be a note to give with as much definiteness as possible the residence, section, township and range. The very point that my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) has mentioned was discussed in the committee. I myself brought the matter up, because in our western country men have to go sometimes

fifteen or twenty miles for their mail, and I thought that might cause confusion.

The Government ask a great deal of us when they -ask us to vote for a Bill of such a nature as this-I will not say of such a suspicious nature, because I want to be court opus-and trust to its being carried out properly because there will be a little note attached. I would as soon the note were left off, because no one knows what kind of a note it will be before it is done with. I would rather legislate in such a definite manner that notes would be unnecessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The requirement of the Bill as it stands is that a man shall give his address. What we had in mind was his address as definitely as he possibly could give it. There can be no objection to inserting in the form that he Shall give his address as definitely as it is possible for him to do. We contemplated that if a man lived in a place where they had streets and numbers ihe would give these or that if he lived in a rural section, he would give the section and range, so as to enable the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to ascertain what electoral district that was in. Of course, notwithstanding all that, there might be cases where a man would not succeed in giving a sufficiently definite address, and unfortunately that man would lose his vote. Under any system there are men who, through errors and mistakes, lose their votes, and all we can do is to provide the best possible machinery to enable men to secure their votes. That there will be mistakes in connection with it by which some will lose their votes I suppose we will have to admit, but I am quite ready to specify as minutely as we possibly can the information that we want each man to give.

That course applies not only to the western provinces; it applies in a degree to the province of Ontario as well. In the constituencies in Ontario we have registration. There are scores of voters in many counties who are not on the list at all. They are not on the list until registration is called within thirty days of polling. Therefore, the same difficulty might arise in Ontario that arises in the West where they have no Tegular voters' list. If being on the voters' list is the qualification, there are plenty of young men who are not qualified in the province of Ontario. There are hundreds of young men in Ottawa from various ridings in Ontario. Does the Bill mean
[Mr. R. B. Bennett. 3
that these young men, unmarried, with no plane of .residence, whose residence is wherever they are if they are not living with their parents, will ibe added to the Ottawa voters' list if they have been here for thirty days?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It means prior to enlistment.
We want to be careful as to what constitutes enlistment.
Taking the oath.

Several men went to the centres and were not formally enlisted until quite a while after they arrived there. Unless great care is exercised the result of the election in these Ontario constituencies may be altogether changed by soldiers' votes. My view is that men- particularly young men-who are at any centre ought to be compelled to have their votes registered at the place where they reside, or where they would be entitled to vote had they not enlisted at all. That situation is just as acute in Ontario as it is in the western provinces. In some of the other provinces it may not be the case, but where we have registration we have many voters who are not qualified if being on the list is their qualification. These should be protected in their right to vote.
Registration only applies to cities in Ontario.
Not to towns?
Towns of over 10,000 or something of that kind.
I think it is 9,000.

There are large towns in which there is no registration. In Welland, Which is not a city, there is no registration. In the city of Niagara Falls there is registration, and that is the only municipality in Welland county in which there is registration. Large numbers of young men have gone from Welland and other urban municipalities in the county of Welland to the war. These young men at the present time are on the voters' list, or a large number of them are. When the voters' list comes to be revised this present year, in August or September, what is to be done with these young men? They are not residents. The provincial Voters' Lists Act requires that they cannot be on the voters' list unless they are resident. Are you proposing by a clause of this Bill to say that there shall be a separate voters' list made out, Which

will be called a Dominion franchise list, and which shall contain the names of the soldiers? If that is not done the names of these young men will be struck off the provincial list and they will not have a vote for the provincial legislature. Why Should they not have a vote for the provincial legislature as well as for the Dominion Parliament? If these young men are at the war they are struck off the provincial voters' list, and if there is a provincial election they are debarred from voting for candidates for the provincial legislature. They have a vote in the Dominion election if they swear as to their residence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Sections 157 and 158 of the Election Act as it now stands, I think, protect a man who is prevented from being present and getting registration because of his absence on military duty. Section 157 provides that:
Notwithstanding anything contained in any Act of Parliament or in any Act of a provincial legislature, no person otherwise qualified to vote at an election of a member to serve in the House of Commons shall be incompetent to vote at such election by reason only of his having been absent from the electoral district in which such election is held, on account of his serving with or being attached to any corps despatched from Canada for military service, or performing military service within Canada, whether as an officer, a non-commissioned officer or a private, or in any other capacity, or while serving His Majesty in any military capacity, or acting as a war correspondent in connection with any war in which a Canadian contingent is serving.
Section 158 says:
From any oath which any person tendering his vote at such an election may be required to take, there shall, in the case of any person within the meaning of the preceding section, be omitted any statements as to residence which such person cannot by reason of such absence as aforesaid truthfully make-

That only gives him the right to vote if he is on the list. What about the fact of his being struck off the list in the revision? He would be struck off. He cannot stay on because he is an absentee. There is nothing in the Voters' List Act of Ontario which will allow him to stay on if he is serving at the front.
Yes, there is.
They can vote if they are on, but it does not put them on.
They will not be struck off, because they are in the same class as sailors, lumbermen and fishermen. Their absence as soldiers counts for residence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think there is a provision in the Ontario Act covering their case and providing that their names shall be kept on the list. I have sent for the Act.
It may be that in the Ontario Act they are covered, but not in the Dominion Act.
Ontario is not the whole Dominion; there are Manitoba, Saskatchewan and the other provinces.

A man's name cannot be struck off the Ontario list by virtue of the fact that he is only temporarily absent. So long as he Tetains his domicile his name goes on the list. In the particular case under review his name would go on the Ontario list by virtue of the Ontario Act; he being a sailor or a soldier the assessor must still keep his name on the list.
I was not sure that the exception in the Ontario Act applied to soldiers; I know it does apply to sailors and lumbermen.

What would happen in the case of a young man who, in the interval has attained the age of twenty-one years, but who has not been on any voters' list because while he was at home he was not twenty-one years. He could not be struck off the list by the assessor because he was not on the list, but had he remained at home he would have become a voter, in cities where there is registration.

I had the idea when I read this Bill first that it qualified every young man of twenty-one years, who is a British subject, but it appears it does not. - There must be thousands of our young men serving in the forces who would not be qualified under this Bill. For example, if one of my constituents goes to Haliiax and enlists at the barracks there, he may have been only one day in Halifax and not thirty days, and not being on the list in the constituency from which he came, he would not have the right to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He must have been in some constituency thirty days before he enlisted. He may have been only one day in Halifax but he was thirty days in Guys-borough, and he woulu be qualifaeu in that constituency. If you can conceive the case of a man who cannot locate himself anywhere for thirty days of course, he would not be entitled to vote.

There has been a large
enlistment in the province of Quebec, which took place mostly in the cities of Montreal and Quebec, but in the eastern part of the province some of the men went over to New Brunswick and enlisted there. What will happen to men from rural districts who enlisted in Montreal and Quebec, and the Quebec men who enlisted in New Brunswick, who were not voters in their own ridings when they left home? Some of these men, for example, remained around Montreal for a long time, perhaps more than a month, waiting for medical examination and so on. What would happen under such circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The man who came to
Montreal, for example, was a voter in some other electoral district or he was not. If he was a qualified voter in some other electoral district he continues on the list, and his qualification as a soldier will be as a voter in that district. If he was not a voter in another district when he came to Montreal, and he resided in Montreal for thirty days before he enrolled, then, under this Act, he will become a voter in that electoral district in Montreal in which he resided during these thirty days. Anything he does after he has enlisted does not affect in any way the district in which he is to vote. The fact that he went to New Brunswick and enlisted there does not affect it at all, because he will be attached either to the electoral district in which before enlistment he was a qualified voter, or if he was not a qualified voter in any district his vote will be assigned to the place in which he resided for thirty days before he enlisted.

I assume from what
the minister says that if he was in Montreal for thirty days before he enlisted he would be placed as a voter in Montreal, but suppose he was in Montreal only twenty-eight days, would he be a voter in the part of the country in which he had formerly resided?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I understand it, he will vote in any electoral district in which he had resided for not less than thirty days before he enlisted.

There will be eleven ridings upon the island of Montreal next election, and supposing this man while waiting in Montreal to be enlisted shifted his residence around between different con-
stituencies during the thirty days. I suppose that one-half of those who enlisted were young men and were not voters at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If a man is so much ot a rolling stone that he cannot find an electoral district in which he lived for thirty days, I am afraid he will have to do without his vote.
He may have been in Montreal for the thirty days, but he may have lived between one constituency and another.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If he was in Montreal for thirty days and he cannot locate himself in one electoral district for thirty days, I fear he will have no vote.
Is not that an injustice to him?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Would it be fair to an electoral district to allot to it a man who has resided in it only two days? We have got to get a limit of some kind, and you can conceive all imaginable eases such as are suggested where a man will not meet the requirements, but it all comes back to this: is it a reasonable requirement to ask that a man should be thirty days in an electoral district in order to look upon him as so attached to that district as to entitle him to vote there? The pointing out of the fact that persons who do not comply with this disposition will not get votes, does not seem to be an argument against this provision of the Bill. If the provision be open to criticism, I should have thought it would come from the direction that thirty days was not long enough, and not from the point of view that because a man has travelled from one electoral 'district to another during the thirty days he will not get a vote. Under the franchise law in the provinces generally, some period of residence much longer than thirty days is required for a man to get a vote in that district. A man may have lived in Montreal for years, but if he is like the supposed soldier of my hon. friend (Mr. Mar-cil) and has been flitting from one to the other of the electoral districts, so that he has not lived the precise period in any one district, such a man would have no vote. For the benefit of the soldier we have reduced the required period of residence down to what I think is a fair minimum.
I do not think we could be expected to meet the case of a man who has had no local habitation for a period of thirty days.

The Montreal lists are made, as the Minister of Justice knows,

every two years in December. Regardless of a man's length of residence in the district, if he has a domicile even for one day prior to the date when the lists are made out, if he registers he is on the list and entitled to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman say that he need not have any period of residence in the district?

He resides in the city of Montreal. But suppose that the day before the 20th of December, when the lists are made out, he moves from one district in Montreal to another district in Montreal. He registers, giving his domicile at the number and street to which he has moved. He goes on the list, and in any election after that he votes as domiciled at that street and number, no matter where he actually lives.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is quite true. Everybody who is on the list to-day is a competent elector for the next two years in the district upon whose list his name appears.

Suppose that a man is on the list in the city of Montreal, that list being good for two years. That man moves to a rural district where a revision takes place every year in September. He has his principal residence in the rural district. Will the minister tell me that that man has the right to vote in Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the law as it stands you have the principle of one man one vote, and a man is not entitled to cast two votes.
Then, where will such a man vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is putting forward something of a conundrum.
But the law solves that conundrum. It says that a man votes where his principal place of residence is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Is that material to our present question? I did not come here this morning prepared to determine all the possible questions that might arise in all the laws of all the provinces. But, in answer to the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Verville), I would point out that, eliminating the case of a man who has become a voter somewhere else, and dealing with the people who live in Montreal, the man who is to-day on the electoral list of a particular electoral division of Montreal, is a voter in that 14-3	.
division for the next two years. If he presented himself at the poll, his name would be found upon the list, and, subject to objection that might be taken by reason to his being entitled to vote elsewhere, prima facie, he is a voter in the electoral district. Therefore, so far as the city of Montreal is concerned, and the flitting of people from one electoral district to another within the city, I do not think there is occasion to apprehend difficulty in the application of this Act. A man who has gone to the front has not gone to a rural district and acquired a residence. So, the case the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) suggested can hardly arise.
The families of those who have families may move: the residence changes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend is
tackling a very large question now. There is a very material difference in meaning between domicile and residence.
Well, I will use the word " domicile."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I must decline to enter into a discussion upon such very fine points as the definition of what constitutes domicile and what constitutes residence. If this Bill is to be dealt with, it must be dealt with realizing that after all it will have to operate under the law
12 noon, as it stands. I do not pretend to be able to indicate in advance just how, in exceptional and individual cases, it may operate. But, speaking generally as regards the city of Montreal, and the man who to-day is on the list and goes to the front, I am satisfied you will not find as many as one-half of one per cent of eases in which these men will not continue to be qualified electors in the electoral districts upon whose lists their names appear. So, with regard to the people moving from one district to another, which is the case presented by the hon. member for Maison-neuve, I do not think there is any practical difficulty.
men be in? Are they to have the choice where they shall vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand the hon. gentleman is speaking of men who, having enlisted, reside in different districts. I would point out that what takes place after enlistment has no bearing on the question. Thirty days after enlistment, or a year after enlistment, does not affect the matter: it is prior to enlistment.

What force does the hon. gentleman give to the word " immediately " in relation to residence? If a man is twenty or twenty-five days away from his ordinary residence, can he swear that he resided in a certain place for thirty days immediately before the date of his enlistment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Where does the hon. gentleman find the word " immediately "?
In the affidavit, page 6.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The section does not
make the requirement that it should be immediate. The affidavit was apparently copied from a form in the present statute, and I do not think that that word " immediately " should appear therein. However, that will be a question to be considered when we come to deal with the form itself.

The latter part of
this section reads:
Provided that if any person was, at the time he was so appointed, enlisted or enrolled, qualified to vote in any other electoral district in Canada, he shall vote in such other district only.
The question I raised was as to the position in which a young man would be, who, at the time of enlistment, was not enrolled or qualified to be enrolled, but who, between the time of his enlistment and the time of the election, qualified for enrolment. I have a son who, though he was not 21 years of age when he enlisted, is 21 years of age now and is away from the electoral district to which he belongs. How will this provision apply to young men between the ages of 18 and 21 who have enlisted-and there are many of them-and who may in the meantime have become properly qualified to vote if at home?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no doubt that, under the conditions which the hon. member indicates, the young man in question, when he enlisted, was not qualified to vote in any electoral district. The proviso does not entitle him to vote in any particular

district, because he was not qualified to vote there at the time of enlistment. Under the section as it stands, that young man could become a qualified voter only in an electoral district in which he had resided for 30 days prior to his enlistment. I would fancy urat in the majority of cases the district in which such a young man resided 30 days before he enlisted would be the district of his home. There will be cases where that is not so, but hon. gentlemen will remember that the 30 days is a period not beiore leaving this country, but before enlistment.

Immediately prior
to enlistment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It need not necessarily be immediately prior to enlistment; the section of the Act does not say " immediately." I think possibly it may require some little consideration as to whether that word "immediately" should stand in the form or not. Under the operation of this section, a young man in the position mentioned by the hon. member would not have the right to vote in his own home district, because he was not a qualified voter there -when he enlisted.

If he should go
albroad, he would not be entitled to have a vote anywhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He will have a vote if he had resided for thirty days immediately before enlistment in some place in Canada, but if you leave out the word " immediately," which is a matter that I should like to have stand for further consideration, then a man who fulfilled this requirement twenty years ago would 'be entitled to vote.
I am speaking now of young men who have just attained the age of twenty-one years, of which there are quite a number at the front.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
According to the present provisions, a young man who has lived thirty days in Canada will have a vote. I do not think that we can secure that that young man's vote shall 'be in the district of his home, unless the district of his home be the place where he has lived during the required period. We have two classes to deal with: persons who, when they enlisted, were qualified to vote, and persons who, when they enlisted, -were not qualified to vote. In respect of the latter class, I do not think that we can do any better than

give them a vote in the place where they had their residence for the thirty days. The others will have the right to vote in the district in which they are qualified to vote. I think that in the majority of cases it will work out that the provision will give the young man a vote in the place which is his home.

The right hon. Prime Minister this morning [DOT]intimated that he is in sympathy with the suggestion that votes should be given to minors who are at the front. The reasons given for that are the reasons which were elaborated so fully yesterday afternoon and evening, namely that this Government has such a responsive and appreciative feeling for the boys at the front that nothing is too good for them. Hon. gentlemen opposite spoke in eulogistic terms last night of the lads who have gone to the front, in support of the view that any one who is fit to carry a gun surely is fit to cast a vote. If hon. gentlemen opposite accept the view that lads of 16 and 17 should be entitled to vote, I suggest that there is just as much reason for giving the suffrage to the nurses who have gone to the front as there is for giving it to lads under 21. Many persons believe that all women who have reached the age of 21 years should be given the suffrage. We heard hon. gentlemen on the Government side slobber over the soldiers last night; the Prime Minister pointed out how disappointed the fathers and mothers would be if this privilege were not granted to the soldiers. It is my belief that the Prime Minister cares not so much for the mothers as he does for the fathers and brothers, especially those who have a vote. I am not going to slobber over the nurses; enough slobbering was done yesterday. I contend that girls and women who risk their lives to perform work that men cannot do, for the good of their country and the honour of civilization, have just as much right to vote as lads of 16 and 17 have.
. I myself am not very far from being a supporter of woman suffrage, but I shall not raise that question on the present occasion. I do say that if you are going to give the vote to boys of 16, 17 and 18, you should give it to the girls who have gone out there to do this great work. Surely a cheap, slobbering desire to get votes is not all that is left to us; surely we are gallant enough and chivalrous enough to say that votes shall be given to these women 143*
as well as to the boys and men. If the Government are going to go ahead with this burlesque measure, they should take it into their serious consideration whether they should not give votes to these women who, in many cases at great sacrifice, have gone to the front to carry on this noble work.
We in the Dominion of Canada would then stand out before the world as showing our appreciation in a very unique way, not in a vote-catching way-because I think the women would not vote as the Minister of Public Works has suggested, but would vote pretty squarely, and I do not think you could monkey with their votes- and would do itself credit by thus showing its appreciation of the women who have gone out, especially in the Red Cross work, and would thus encourage others to enlist in that noble service.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I gave credit to the hon. gentleman for not having slobbered over the nurses and also for a disinclination to monkey with the women's votes. I further take note of his request that the Government should take the suggestion into consideration, and beg to assure him that the Government shall give it its most serious consideration.

While we are speaking on this question of giving votes to young men who have not reached their majority of 21 years, because they are going to the front, we should remember that there are other young men who have not gone to the front, but who are possibly as useful to the war as those who have gone. You will find many young men to-day who are supporters of families, who are working in different factories, making shells and other things that are necessities of war; and if you are going to give the right to vote to these young men because they are going to the front it is absolutely unfair not to give it to other young men here of the same age. You will find such young men in many industries to-day throughout Canada, even on the farm. I do not care where it is, these young men are producers of different things that are keeping our soldiers at the front, whether they are producing money to support the affairs of the country or manufacturing different articles that are necessary for the war. If we want to be fair we should not give the vote only to young men who are going to the front. Lower the limit to 18 years if you like, but give the vote to these other young men.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would ask the hon. gentleman to give a little further explanation of his position. The suggestion to give votes to young men under 21 years of age stands for further consideration this afternoon; but, because I would like in that consideration clearly to apprehend the view of the hon. gentleman, I would be glad if he would tell me whether I am correct in understanding that he does not consider that the alteration in the Bill withdrawing the requirement of 21 years should be made; or does he think that we ought to do it with regard to the soldiers and also with regard to the other young men he speaks of?

My suggestion is that if we are going to grant the vote to soldiers of less than twenty-one years of age, we should also grant the vote to other young men in the country who are also working for the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I really would be glad to know what the hon. gentleman's view is as to the desirability of giving votes to soldiers who are under twenty-one years, because that is a matter that we have to consider practically. I understand he says if we do that we ought also to give it to other young men. But I would be glad to know whether he thinks we ought to do that.
The Government can give the vote as much as they like; it makes no difference to me, provided they make no exceptions and are fair with everybody.

If there is to be any enlargement of the scope of the Bill to include parties not now mentioned in it, I think the minister ought to consider the case of. the sailors who are engaged in the mercantile trade of the North Atlantic. At the present time that is a very dangerous pursuit. Everybody knows that a ship cannot arrive at a British port to-day without risking the lives of heT crew. That service is almost as dangerous now as service in the navy or in the trenches. I know of many young men who are manning our ships which are carrying food and supplies to the Allies at the present time. They sleep with their clothes on, with the boats hung over the side of the ship ready to jump into them, .they are expecting the torpedo to strike their ship, all through the long night. It is a most anxious time with those men, and if the Bill is to be enlarged so as to take in parties not now 
included, 1 would suggest that the Government ought to consider the cases of those thousands of men engaged in the mercantile service on the Atlantic ocean.

What is the difference between enlistment and enrollment? A recruiting officer was sent from New Brunswick into my constituency. He visited different parishes and took the names of a number of people who did not actually move away with mim, but who ultimately left, and, when they had undergone medical examination and other formalities, were included in the forces. What is the difference between enlistment and enrollment? Is this to be reckoned from the date the recruiting officer first appeared in the constituency or from the date on which the engagement was completed in New Brunswick, perhaps some weeks afterwards. It would make a difference as to whether the voter would belong to his own county or to the new county.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The 30 days are counted as from the appointment, which I understand is the proper term for any person joining the force as an officer. I must confess that I am not absolutely clear on the terminology, but I understand that when a man first presents himself he is enlisted and takes an oath. After he has undergone medical examination and complied with other formalities he is then enrolled. It might perhaps have been sufficient to mention enlistment only, but I presume there might be a case where a man would be immediately enrolled for one reason or another and this was only to make quite certain that the 30 days is to date from whichever event occurred first.

I think it might be advisable for the Minister of Justice to take the opinion of the Militia Department on the use of these words. As I understand, as a practical man with some experience, a man is enlisted when he first signs. In order to complete his enlistment he has to pass the doctors and certain preliminaries. He has to take the oath of allegiance. Then he signs his name to the service roll and that completes his enlistment. The adjutant puts his name on the book and it is sent to headquarters. He then becomes a regular member of the militia, his term of service i3 three years and he becomes lia-able to military law. I rather think that the word " enrolled" should be struck out. It is superfluous and does not add to the meaning or to the strength of the section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would be very glad to act on the suggestion of the hon. member; I have no doubt his description is correct. Subject to the verification by the Militia - Department of the suggestion made it would seem to me that the word "enrolled" probably is superfluous. It was doubtless put in there as a result of too much precaution. Certainly the intention is that the 30 days should be before whatever is the first step in making him a soldier.
When he gives in his name.

I wish to draw the minister's attention to one class of men to whom it is proposed to give votes under this Bill. A British subject living in the United States may make up his mind to go home to England to fight with the British army. He has been some time away from England, and has no vote there. Although he has lived in the United States for a long time, he has not taken out his papers, and so has no vote there. Before he goes over to England he learns that the Canadian soldiers are paid $1.10 a day, while the soldiers in Britain are paid only 25 cents. So he crosses the border with the intention of joining the Canadian forces. But he is delayed for thirty days in this country before he enlists. This man is a British subject who had originally intended to join the English army. He has no particular interest in Canada exoept that it is a part of the Empire. He has joined the Canadian forces in order to get the better pay, which he is perfectly justified in doing. Now, because that man happened to live in Canada for thirty days before enlisting the minister proposes to give him a vote. I appeal to the minister whether that is a reasonable thing to do. The man knows absolutely nothing about Canadian politics.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Even if that be a very great evil, I hardly think it will happen in a large number of cases.
Not in many cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We have always Ito
make laws under which we are going to find hard cases that will come up. Almost any law it is natural though perfectly just in its application in the great bulk of cases is liable to give rise to anomalies in isolated cases; but I hardly think that that is a reason why we should not be prepared to adopt a law that in the great general sense will give a vote to the man who is a Canadian and a member of the Canadian forces.
After all, what we do is this. We assume that the man who becomes a Canadian soldier does so because he is interested in Canada; he gives the most tangible, prima facie evidence of interest in Canada. There may be an odd man who joins the Canadian forces to get $1,10 a day instead of the 25 cents which he would get in Great Britain; and if we could get at the motives of every individual man perhaps we ought to make a distinction and not give that man a vote. But I suggest that it is not a practicable thing to draw that distinction, and, after all, no material evil can result from a few isolated cases such as my hon. friend has: mentioned. After all, the hon. gentleman speaks of him as a man who wants to fight for Britain. Well, in this particular condition of affairs the man who wants to fight for Britain, and fights for Britain, wants to fight for Canada, and is fighting for Canada.

Has the minister given
any consideration to the hundreds of Frenchmen living in Canada who are nowfighting under the French flag? There have been hundreds of these men in Montreal. They are British subjects, but descendants of French parents. I could name hundreds who have been called back to fight with the French army; members of the Bar and of almost every other profession have gone back to France from Montreal. The city engineer of Montreal, Mr. Janin, who was through the whole campaign of 1870, is going back now at the age of 62. Has tlhe minister given any consideration to this class of men?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Consideration has been given to it. Although the gentlemen indicated may have become naturalized, they are undoubtedly people who, under the operation of the different laws in the different countries, find themselves with a double nationality; otherwise they would not be called upon to return to the colours of France. Finding themselves with that double nationality, and recognizing their obligations as citizens of the French Republic, it seems to me that we cannot do otherwise than assume that they have made their choice as between these two nationalities. I am not criticising them for having done that, but they have done it. Being entitlea to be French cittizens or British subjects, or both so far as they can consistently be both, when the time comes for action they choose to range themselves as French citizens.
The cause is the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The cause is the same,
but if we are going to give votes to all who are fighting for that cause we shall have to extend the Bill to all the soldiers in all the armies of the Anies. It seems to me that the action of these men has settled for the time being what is their national status, and while I should be glad to recognize in a proper way the fidelity that these men have shown to their original country by returning to take their places in the ranks of its army, I hardly think that the proper way of recognizing that fidelity would be to give them the franchise of the country which they have made clear that they consider, as between the two, the secondary country. There would be this further difficulty in the way. We do not propose to give a vote to the man in the armies of Great Britain who may have some connection with Canada. In dealing simply with members of the Canadian forces, we have the advantage that we are dealing with men who, while they are serving as a part of the Imperial army, are men organized as Canadians, and organized to a very large extent, though not entirely, under Canadian officers. We are dealing with organizations with regard to which it is more easy for us to create a system which we can hope to have carried out, than if we endeavoured to ask for cooperation on the part of officers of the armies of totally different countries- countries which, though our Allies, and though we respect them as such, are nevertheless absolutely distinct countries.

I should just like to say a word for the Belgian colony in Montreal.
I do not wish to add anything further to what I have said about the French reservists, except to say that these men are Canadians and will come back to Canada after the war is over. The same thing applies to the Belgian colony of Montreal, which sent over 1,000 men to Belgium. These men have taken part in the campaign, but they will lose their votes simply because they are not members of the Canadian forces.

This Bill opens up a question that I have discussed with friends of mine for some time past. I should like to ask the Minister of Justice if there is any clause in this Bill dealing with what might be called absentee voters. There are thousands of voters in the Dominion of Canada who are disfranchised, who have nd vote, simply because they do

not happen to be in the locality; they have left their homes where their names appear on the voters' list, they have moved away perhaps one hundred miles. They are bona fide voters who have lost their votes because they have moved to places where there is no registration, and there is no registration except in cities or towns of a certain population. A workman who is away from home, for instance, has no vote where he is located, he cannot afford to pay his way back to vote at	his	own poll,	and	the	candidateis	not	allowed to	pay	his	expenses.
The consequence is that the man is disfranchised. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice is putting into force machinery to record the votes of the soldiers who may be in the trenches, tout I am perfectly satisfied that very much more simple machinery would suffice to record the vote of the man who is still a resident of Canada, but who, from the fact of his being a distance from home, is unable to record his vote. There is another case even simpler than that to which I have referred, and that is the case of a man who moves out of one county to an adjoining county,
, and he happens to move out of the county in which he was a resident after the voters' list is completed. He moves into the new county too late to be placed on the list in that county, and when the election takes place he is disfranchised. I am satisfied that the minister could put a clause in this Bill to deal with the absentee vote, protecting the right of the bona fide voters who have not moved out of the Dominion. They have their residence in some part of the Dominion, but owing to their having moved away and not being able to pay their expenses toack home they are disfranchised. The same thing applies to the man who has moved out of one county into another and who, because he is too late to be put on the voters' list in the county into which he has moved, is disfranchised.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no doubt that there is very much in what the hon. gentleman has pointed out. The adoption of his suggestion would result in the establishment in this country of laws similar to those which have been enacted in a number of countries providing special provisions for the absentee vote, or as it is sometimes called the postal vote. In looking into different matters in connection with the present Bill I must say that I have formed a very favourable impression of the possibility of such a provision being carried

out. The measure which is now proposed is the first step in that direction. Perhaps it might very properly be said that the reasons for providing for this method of voting in this particular case are stronger than they are in support of a general system, but this is one step in that direction. We are providing a method for the albsent voter, and if this should work out as satisfactorily as we hope it will I certainly would foe disposed to look very favourably upon some measure to remedy the evils which the hon. gentleman has mentioned.

Some time ago, when questions were put to the Minister of Justice as to the effect of this law as applied to the different voters' qualifications in the different provinces, he brushed the matter aside by saying that he was not going to undertake to describe the limitations or applications of the law under all possible circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think that I
brushed it aside, or that I would not pay attention to it. It seemed to me that the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) was rather refining the distinctions and I said that I did not come here, and that I did not pretend to be prepared, to deal with all the niceties and distinctions of the law. I said that I was endeavouring, of course in a general way, to make thi" iaw so operate as not to produce anomalies by reason of the conditions of the laws in the different provinces. I shall be very glad to have anything pointed out to me in regard to the law of any province which might call for a modification of any provision of this Bill.

Perhaps the minister has misunderstood the point I was trying to get at. I do not wish to criticise what he said but I wish to take his expressions as giving the main reasons for the criticism that I find against his Bill and particularly against this section. It undertakes to define certain rights. It defines them, if I may say so, in a very indefinite way as will be found to be the case when these definitions come to be applied to the different conditions throughout the provinces. That this is the best that can be done, we admit, but that being the condition, the circumstances under which the vote is taken, absolutely preclude the ordinary safeguards that guarantee both to the voter who votes, and his fellow citizens, that his vote shall be cast according to the rights that he holds. On
these points the minister does not feel himself able to present any opinion to this House and therefore the individual voter is the sole judge of his action in regard to them. That is not a fair proposition. That is not right. It is essentially wrong that it should be the ease. In the ordinary circumstances of the election law, in the first place, the right of the voter is defined as definitely as words can define it. Beyond that there is a procedure laid down guaranteeing to the electors generally, as well as to the voter, that while he shall have the benefit of the rights conferred upon him by the Act, he shall not go beyond those rights -he shall be kept within those limits. That is not possible under the conditions set out in this Act; at any rate, there has not been provided that machinery, that procedure, to safeguard the public against the misuse of the right of the franchise. The voter himself is the sole judge as to where his rights shall rest. If the Minister of Justice finds difficulty in deciding on that point, how much more is the voter liable to take a view that is not warranted by the law and is not according to the intent of the law? My hon. friend may ask: What is the practical objection to it? The practical objection is this: In his earlier remarks, when we were discussing this proviso, the minister pointed out very clearly and very properly that it was the object of the law that there should not be an undue disorganization of the strength of the voting population, that matters, in so far as voting was concerned, should remain as much as possible as they were. That is perfectly right but by reason of the indefiniteness of the law in prescribing the exercise of the right of the franchise it will be entirely possible to mass the votes in this direction or in that in large measure and so produce that very disorganization which the minister stated was undesirable and which it was the purpose of the law to avoid. That is to say, the minister has undertaken to deal with a vastly important subject and he has not provided the machinery to deal with that subject according to the principle he himself has laid down. He may answer that it is impossible to provide that procedure, and that is the very point upon which we take issue. We say that if the rights of the franchise are not to be exercised with due regard to the right of the public as well as to the rights of the voter, then the right of the public should prevail.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the- hon. member's
own province, if one of these soldiers were

at home, he would walk into the polling-booth and he would swear to his own qualification, and to his qualification in a particular district, and he would then be allowed to vote.
Sure. '

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Now, we are requiring
of that same soldier voter, who happens not to be at home, that he should swear to these very same things. The criticism of the hon. member of the sufficiency of the safeguards for the soldiers voting as proposed by this Bill, apply absolutely to the safeguards provided under the general law with regard of the votes of the voters in the province of Alberta. So far as that province is concerned, we require from the absent soldier all that would be required from him if he were at home and voted. As regards the other provinces where there is a system of lists established, there is a method of checking the statement of a man who is a qualified voter in a certain district. I do not think there is any less safety in the respect pointed out by the hon. member in the manner in which this soldiers' vote is to be taken than there is in the manner in which the ordinary vote is to be taken in certain parts of the Dominion. There was a suggestion made by the committee which had the consideration of these election matters that the law under which a man may give his vote in Alberta by merely swearing to his qualifications should be repealed, and when that provision came to the House we found that the opinion of all the members from that province, and a large number of others also, was that under the conditions in that province it would not be fair to repeal that law, and that in order that a man should be fairly treated there, it was essential that that principle should prevail which allowed men to vote upon their own affidavits as to their own qualifications. Surely the conditions under which our soldiers find themselves ought to be considered sufficient to justify that the same principle be applied in their case.

I am sorry to prolong the discussion, but I am compelled to point out that in the case of the ordinary Alberta voter at the ordinary election there is only one question of his qualification, and all he has to answer to decide on his vote is whether he resided in a certain electoral district or whether he did not. Under this legislation the voter has two things to do; he has to decide as to whether 
he must vote under his term of enlistment, or under his former residence, and that is a radical and important difference. There is another difference, and it is that the voter who comes into the poll to cast his vote in an ordinary Alberta election does so under circumstances, and conditions, and procedure,1 framed especially for the purpose of safeguarding him in the exercise of his right, and of taking proceedings against him should he go beyond that right. There is no provision in this Act for taking the same measures of precaution in the case of the soldier voting, nor is there any possibility of such precautions being taken. The two cases are not by any means alike and the difference is so great as to warrant my suggestion that the minister has undertaken to do something that it is not possible to do. The minister has undertaken to give a right to a certain man to which he certainly^ is entitled, but he has to give it to him under such circumstances that he cannot protect the right of the body politic.
At one o'clock, the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

As I understand it, the purpose of the section now before the committee is to provide that those of the active forces abroad who are qualified to vote at the time they enlisted shall be afforded means of casting their vote. But the form of oath provided in the Bill does not seem to apply to all cases. The form of oath is " that immediately before I was enlisted m the military forces of Canada I was qualified to 'be a voter." But a great many of the persons supposed to be enfranchised by that Act cannot take that oath. If this law is to become operative it will be necessary to make some slight change in the form of affidavit.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will observe that there are two paragraphs in the form of affidavit given. The first is for the soldier who is enfranchised under this Act, the other is for the soldier who is already qualified to vote in a particular district.
As I understand it, it does not say anything about the qualification in the first paragraph.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, because all that is required for his qualification is that he should be a British subject, twenty-one years of age, and should have resided for

[DOT]3273
thirty days in some particular location in Canada before enlisting. If, on the other hand, he was, apart from being a soldier, qualified s a voter in a particular district, he will swear to the second paragraph, leaving out the other.

It was hinted that we were able to legislate in this Parliament with regard to the men who would go to the front, but that once a volunteer goes from our shores and gets to the other side, he goes under control of the British War Office, which places him in such regiment or elsewhere as it may think proper. There is no such body known to the law as the Canadian military service. Our military forces, when they get to the other side, are scattered among as many Tegiments and battalions as is deemed proper. As I understand it, there is no entity in the army today which can !be called a Canadian contingent or Canadian military force. I submit that the term the minister used in the Act is somewhat speculative, to say the least. If this law were one to confer the franchise upon the militia force of Canada, there is such a body recognized by the Militia Act. But the force that we send out is a force of volunteers who, of their own volition and without compulsion of the Government, became part and parcel of the British army. Therefore, I submit, we have no jurisdiction to follow the volunteer into the position in which he puts himself; we can only leave him to the control of the British army, and the British army law, until such time as he is released and comes back. I submit that Parliament i'S asked to legislate for a body that does not exist at all. I do not hesitate to put anyself on record here-I dad not speak on the second reading of the Bill-as toeing opposed to the measure. I believe that it is not workable and that it will only add to the difficulties already existing at the front. The soldiers when they go to the front take upon themselves certain responsibilities, and we repose certain trusts in them. They are to do the fighting for us, and ive are to provide for them in every way that we can. Their minds are not to toe bothered about political or municipal affairs; they must have a free band to deal with the very arduous and important matters they have -before them. On the other hand, the soldier has to trust to the friends whom he leaves behind and to the people of the country that in his absence political matters shall toe kept on an even keel. As we trust them at the front,
they have to trust us here. The one argument put forward is that the soldier is entitled to exercise the franchise. There may be some argument in that so far as the soldier who had the right to the franchise before he left his home is concerned. It might be said: You are depriving the soldier of the right which he would toe able to exercise if he were at home. While it would, perhaps, be desirable to let the soldier who was a voter at home vote abroad, if that could be done in the right way, we are not called upon to create a new franchise in order to give votes to persons who could not vote if they were at home. I am opposed to this Bill because I do not think that it provides for a method whereby the soldiers may vote as they ought to vote. A person who expresses his opinion at the ballot box is in a somewhat similar position to the man who sits on a jury. If the minister were on the bench, and, as he was about to charge the jury, one of the jurors came in and took his place, he would say to that juror: You have not heard the evidence, and you are not in a position to give a verdict in this case. He would thereupon either order a new trial, or direct the juror, leave the box. This is what would toe done in a case where persons are called upon to decide upon the facts, and an election is the highest sphere in which the people are called upon to decide upon the facts. The men to whom if is proposed to give votes are away from this country, and will be away perhaps a year or eighteen months, or two years, before they are called upon to exercise their franchise under this Act. They know nothing about the changes that have taken place in this country since they went away; they know nothing about the conduct of the Government since that time. They are deprived of the privilege of voting for the representative. A strong and eloquent plea was made the other night against granting to the man who received the minority vote in a constituency the right to take a seat in Parliament, for the reason that he was not the choice of the people. I agree, to a certain extent, with that view; yet under this proposed legislation we are called upon to give the right to vote to men who are far away from home, who are out of touch with the issues that will be threshed out in an election, and who have no knowledge of the qualifications of the candidates. Without taking shelter behind the assertion that I am not opposed to voting by soldiers, or behind any other shelter, I say that I am absolutely opposed to this

Bill, and, so far as the soldiers who are my friends at 'the front are concerned, I take the responsibility of felling them that I do not think that this legislation is right or necessary. I am sure that the soldiers are not asking for it, and do not expect it.
Section stands.
On section 2-distribution of ballot papers:

The soldiers may be
divided into two classes, those who are in Canada and those who are outside of Canada. I see no reason why the soldiers who are in Canada at the time of an election cannot vote under the ordinary machinery and subject to the ordinary restrictions and regulations that are now in force. There is no reason why the deputy returning officer should not take the votes of the soldiers in the different localities in which they are stationed, and forward them to the constituencies to which they belong. Take the city of Ottawa: there could be one or two polls for the soldiers only. The votes could be recorded by the deputy returning officer, under the usual conditions and subject to the usual safeguards as now provided, and afterwards be sent to the proper constituency. There is another feature of this matter to which I think the attention of the minister ought to be directed. Several of the officers to whom these ballots will be sent for distribution and who, under this Act, will take the votes of the soldiers, are now or will be candidates for election to this House. It is not impugning their honesty, or anything of that kind, to point out the anomaly that will exist if men act as returning officers and handle votes that are cast for or against themselves. I imagine that no one of the officers to whom I refer would care to be placed in a position of that kind, and i mink that some provision ought to be made by which in no case shall an officer who is himself a candidate be a returning officer or have anything to do with the ballots. These are the two points which I wish to impress strongly upon the minister in connection with this section of the Bill.. First, there is no need for all this machinery for the casting of the votes of soldiers who are in Canada; they could be taken with our ordinary machinery without removing any safeguards; and, secondly, no man should be allowed to handle ballots who is a candidate in an election.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is much that
commends itself to one's judgment in the suggestion made by my hon. friend with
{Mr. McKenzie.]
respect to soldiers who are at home. In the committee we endeavoured to deal with the soldier vote as a whole and it is possible we did not give sufficient attention to the difference in methods necessary for those at home and those abroad. Would the hon. member contemplate that soldiers, say at Quebec or Halifax, whose votes would have to be sent to distant electoral districts should vote on the election day or sufficiently before the regularly appointed election day to allow of their ballots reaching their destinations by the polling day?

I did not think out the details, but personally I would see no objection to having a polling day for the soldiers which would be sufficiently early to permit of their ballots reaching their home constituencies before the regular polling day. Of course it would be all secret and no person would know anything about the ballots until the close of the general poll.

The difficulty
pointed out in that scheme is that in some cases it would be physically impossible for the soldiers to vote after nomination day and still have their votes reach their home electoral districts on election day. In most parts of Canada the matter could be worked out, but there would be great difficulty in regard to Vancouver troops who might be at Halifax, and it would be impossible for the votes of Victoria soldiers who might be at Halifax to be cast after nomination day and be received in the home constituency -..ore polling day. It could be worked except for constituencies west of the Rockies.
It would work out with the great majority of voters anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I suppose the vote might be taken on nomination day?
There was some discussion as to their knowing who the candidates were.

I am opposed to this Bill, more particularly to clause 2, because I do not see any possible way in which the votes can be taken fairly so that there can be any certainty that they will be delivered as cast. let us look for a moment how it works out in particular constituencies. In Edmonton the Conservative candidate is the commanding officer. Does the Minister of Justice think that it would operate satisfactorily in a case such as that, where there are hun-

dreds of men brought in from the surrounding constituencies of Alberta, a great many of whom will be there long enough to qualify in Edmonton, but who will also have votes in their home constituencies? These men could vote in Edmonton by securing a half-day off on election day, go out in civilian clothes, take the oath that they were voters in Edmonton, and so cast their votes there. Even granted that a commanding officer who was a Conservative candidate would not care to act as returning officer for his own election, he would appoint somebody under him in the military force to do so. Let me ask, in all candour, is there a man in this House on either side who would want deliberately to put the ballots for his election in the hands of any candidate opposed to him, to let him deliver them or not deliver them just as he saw fit, without more safeguards than have been provided in this Bill? The more the Bill is discussed, the more utterly and absolutely absurd it seems to expect that the votes will be delivered and counted as they were given. If I was reasonably sure that the vote as cast would be delivered, I would hold up both* hands for this Bill. I have a large number of men from my own constituency at the front, two out of three of whom are supporters of my own; but, under the circumstances, scattered, as they may be, in Turkey, Egypt, Bermuda, England, France, Belgium, and I hope in Germany, I would not have one hope in a thousand that their vote would be delivered in Canada at the election as they were intended to be. Who has asked for this legislation, might I ask the minister? We have not been able to hear yet of anybody who has done so. Has any section of the army, has any section of the militia forces asked for this legislation? For my part I do not believe that the Government has any expectation that this will ever become law; and it is all done to enable them to wave the flag that the Liberals were against allowing the soldiers to vote. We are not against allowing the soldiers to vote, but we are against allowing the Government to count the votes after they are cast. The Prime Minister yesterday spoke of the difficulty of getting honest elections in Canada. Let us talk plainly. We know on both sides of the House that there is a great deal of difficulty in getting the votes counted properly, with all the restrictions with which the best men in the country have been able to hedge about the Election Act during the last 50 years. We know what the results are. My right, hon. friend yesterday made some
remark on that line which I will read to the House:
