I recall that with all our safeguards and legislative provisions, a deputy returning officer and a poll clerk went forth in one of our western provinces, pretended to journey into the north 100 or 120 miles, but went in reality only 20 or 30 miles, where they sat down under a tree, filled in 150 names, deposited as many ballots, and came back with the story of a unanimous Liberal vote in that remote part of the constituency. It is impossible to prevent fraud absolutely by legislative enactment.
I think my right hon. friend would have done himself more credit if he had told the whole truth in that connection. We all know that the Liberals suffered by the barefaced rascality which was practised on that occasion. That was the first and only time in the history of Canada that a Government deliberately brushed aside all technicalities. They would not call for a new election when they could have won easily, but they took steps to hand over the seat to a Conservative candidate.
They simply gave back the stolen goods.

Certainly, but did hon. gentlemen opposite ever suggest doing anything of the kind? Only last summer three constituencies were absolutely stolen in the backwoods of Manitoba, and the candidates were all confirmed in their seats. There was no restitution there of the stolen goods, not a bit of it.
Let me tell my hon. friends what took place in my constituency in the last Dominion election that hon. gentlemen opposite had the running of. That was in 1896. At that time we had almost the same system of voting that we have at present. The Elections Act did not contain the provision that enables a man to cast his vote on election day whether his name is on the list or not, the provision which the Minister of Justice and my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) suggested should be struck out only a few days ago-and I quite absolve both of them from having any wrong intention in making that proposal. Several days before the election took place, and after the ordinary pen and ink lists for the polling division had been posted up, men were sent out from the Conservative headquarters in Moosomin to instruct every enumerator throughout the constituency to strike off the list a certain percentage of Liberal names. These men were sent out by the men in charge of the Conservative campaign in that constituency. One of these men, whom I know

very well, went to one of the Conservative enumerators in my constituency and suggested that he should strike off 25 per cent of the Liberal names on the list. The enumerator, as straightforward a man as ever lived, absolutely refused to do it. He sent for me and told me what had been suggested. He said that he told me not because he wanted it blazed abroad, but that my friends in the other divisions should be on the look out for trouble. What happened at the next polling subdivision? The enumerator there, the night before the election, struck off twenty-five Liberal names, and then cleared for parts unknown; so that the next day there was nobody to put the names on the list again. My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson), who was in the same constituency at that time, knows something about it, for he had a somewhat similar experience. When polling day came there was almost a riot in the next town to where I live. They had a rope ready for the enumerator, and if they had found him they were going to drag him through a pond close to the town. But he could not be found. I must say, however, to the credit of the Conservatives in that polling subdivision that we did not lose many votes through it, for afterwards man after man told us that they voted for the Liberal candidate because they would not stand for such work as had been going on.
I point this out to show that with all the safeguards we have, it is possible that an honest vote may not be recorded. What can w'e expect then when the vote is taken thousands of miles away, when the men at the front are not so likely to be as careful as they w'ould be if at home, and when the commanding officers are in many cases candidates ! Suppose the commanding officer hands over the work to somebody beneath him who is looking for promotion and wants to stand in with the powers that be. What is likely to happen? So far as I can see, this Bill provides no penalties for the man who does not send in all the votes, or who misdirects them. There are many ways in which the intention of the voter at the front could be defeated. The more you look at this Bill the more difficulties you see in it; it simply bristles with difficulties from one end to the other. Why is the Minister of Justice so anxious to give votes to the soldiers? He knows that 35 or 40 per cent of the voters of Canada do not take the trouble to vote anyway, and I am sure that some of the soldiers who are to be provided

with votes would not take the trouble to vote if they were at home. On the other hand, many no doubt would like to vote, even at the front, and I for one would like to give them the opportunity of voting. I would hold up both hands for any Bill that would ensure that the votes would be counted as the voters intended.
Again, no hon. member of this House has yet shown that there has been any considerable demand from any part of . the militia for soldiers' votes. There is one certain and easy way of getting over this difficulty. Why does not the Prime Minister do the straightforward, honest and patriotic thing, and say that there shall be no election until the war is over, or until the end of the term of Parliament. Nobody would object to that, and if the war was not over when the end of the term of Parliament came I venture to say that every man in this House would be willing to extend the term of Parliament until the war was over. To my mind, it is an outrage to throw this country into the throes of a general election right in the middle of this war, when every bit of energy in the country is required for conducting that war properly. In this easy way the Prime Minister and his followers could settle the whole difficulty. Why do they not do the decent and patriotic thing, and tell the country straightforwardly that there shall be no election before next session at all events? We have every reason to believe that in a year from now the war will be over and our soldiers back in Canada. But I think that hon. gentlemen opposite do not want the soldiers to have votes when they are back in Canada They would rather not have the votes of the soldiers when they come back. A good deal has transpired in the last two months that could lead one to take that view. Therefore, we find the Government anxious to railroad thjs Bill through the House to give votes to the soldiers and at the same time to provide practically no safeguard which would justify us in the expectation that the votes, as they are given in the firing line, will be delivered in the constituencies where the men come from in the way intended.

I am very glad to hear the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Turriff) make the statement that he is strongly in favour of votes for soldiers. I find that a great many hon. members on this side of the House are in favour of votes for soldiers. The difficulty seems to be to provide the necessary ma-

chinery to have the votes taken and also to provide the necessary safeguards. It does seem to me that there is sufficient legal ability in this House to draft a Bill that will provide the necessary machinery as well as the safeguards.
With some diffidence, I would suggest to the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) certain changes. I approach this question with an open mind. These suggestions have just come into my mind to-day, and it may be that they will be found to be very crude. Sections 2 and 3 perhaps ought to be considered together. They provide for the casting of the votes. Section 2 provides that the envelopes for holding the votes -shall be sent by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to the officer in command of each military base in Canada in which volunteers are serving and also to the office of the High Commissioner for Canada in London. Then, section 3 provides that, on the election being called, the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery shall communicate with the officer commanding the corps in which the volunteer is serving and that the commanding officer shall provide each volunteer with a ballot papeT. That is for the men in Canada. As regards the men in Europe, the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery shall notify the secretary of the High Commissioner of the issuing of -the writ and the secretary shall thereupon send a sufficient number of ballot papers, affidavits and envelopes to the proper officer or officers, and such officer or officers shall give each volunteer entitled to vote a ballot paper, affidavit and envelope.
The provision in regard to the duties of the commanding officer are very crude. We have to consider what men are entitled to this vote. First, we have the body of men in Canada. We will have under training in Canada about 20,000 -men; they will be scattered about-10,000 at Valcartier and perhaps 5,000 at two other camps. Surely some simple means could be provided for taking the votes of these men in camp. The, machinery ought to be -simple and effective for that purpose. Next, we come to the votes of the soldiers in England. We are told that we will have at the base in England 20,000 men. The men in England, with the exception of those who are in the hospitals, are altogether in one place, under efficient military organization and under the control of our Militia Department. The third class comprises the men at the front. I am told by my non. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence (Major General Hughes) that we have 38,000 men at the
front and that number will be raised shortly to 50,000 men. Our men at the front will be in two divisions. They are now in one division. That division is under the command of General Alderson and the Canadian officers and staff under him. These men are assembled close together or within a very few miles. With these men all together, or within a very limited area, there should be no difficulty in taking their votes. Many of my friends who have spoken say that these men are at the fighting line. We are led to believe that these men are engaged absolutely in battle night and day. I am told, and you will see it in the reports that come from the front, that trench work consists of one day in the trenches and two days out of the trenches. If they put in two days in the trenches they have four days out of the trenches. They go back to the base, where they are assembled, and there should be no difficulty while they are there in taking their votes. Of course, I can see that there will be a number of men whose votes it might be difficult to take, but we have to face that fact.
I think the machinery provided under sections 2 and 3 is defective. You start right off, and, as soon as the election is announced, you say that the secretary of the High Commissioner shall take action. What shall he do? He must give instructions to the officers commanding the different corps and units and -send them ballot papers, and they are to carry out these instructions. We know that no civilian can give instructions of any kind to military officers. We know that the military officers at the front could not possibly take any commands, orders or instructions from a civilian like the secretary of the High Commissioner. That would be impossible. Then, remember how difficult it would be for him to find out who are the officers commanding these different units. It is very difficult. For example, in. England there are the hospital corps, the army service corps, the paymaster corps, the divisional corps, the artillery, the ammunition corps, cavalry, and what is called the base or recruiting camp. You have all these different units divided into many different parts and having amongst them many commanding officers. It would be almost impossible for the secretary of the High Commissioner, in the short time allowed him to get the necessary information and even to get the proper postal addresses. By the time he got the inform-

ation changes might be made. Then there is this further consideration: 'he has not been in the habit of communicating with the officers commanding the different units; he has not (been transmitting information to them, and he has not 'been receiving reports from them.
It may 'be asked: how can we work this out effectively? It would seem to me that we have the most perfect machinery possible provided for us now. The Militia Department, or the Militia Council, have control practically of all the Canadian troops in England and at the front. Our paymaster's department is a Canadian department. The paymaster's department, now that it is in proper working order, has proved to be most efficient. They have to communicate directly with every officer commanding the different units and they have to directly put the pay into the pockets of every man at the front and of every man in England. This is a direct channel of communication, not only with every officer commanding every unit but with every man in Canada, at the front or in England. Pay is the most effectual way of communicating with the men. We have there a perfect channel of communication under proper direction.
It has been said that it would not be necessary to have this legislation, if the Prime Minister and the Government would say that no election should be brought on until after the war. I have a firm and honest belief that the Government of this country will not have an election until after the war. I believe their duty at the present time is to carry on the business of the country, but their first and prime duty is to prosecute this war with their full energy and all their ability, and to allow nothing to interfere with that. They have the precedent of England for the adoption of this policy. I am glad to have seen that the Opposition has given to the Government during this session, and during the special war session as well, every assistance in their power to conduct public business without party controversy. But there is this to be considered: suppose the war should end in a year, and a truce be declared, we know very well that our troops would have to stay in Europe after that, for five or six or perhaps eight months, as in South Africa they had to remain for almost a year. Until all the preliminaries are carried out, the indemnities arranged for, and the treaty entered into, our soldiers could not return to Canada, and in the natural course of events, the time for a

general election would come before then.
As I have said, the Militia Department has the most perfect machinery and the most perfect channel of communication to reach effectually every man and every officer at the front. We have provided the soldiers with their clothing, and we are providing their pay, and when promotions are made by General Alderson, he reports at once to the Militia Department here, and every detail at the front is practically arranged through the Militia Department in Canada. My suggestion then is, that the ballot papers should be sent to the secretary of the Militia Council, and that there should be imposed on the Militia Council the duty of forwarding these ballot papers to the proper officers, because they know the commanding officers of the different units, their location, and everything about them. The Militia Council could give the necessary military instructions that would be promptly obeyed by the officers of the different units, and then the
4 p.m. ballot papers could be returned sealed to the Militia Council, to be handed over to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. This, Sir, is my suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have heard with interest the admirable suggestion made by the hon. member (Mr. H. H. McLean). I had in mind, when we come to the section which describes the officers to whom the ballots are to be sent from the Secretary of State, that the officer on the other side who is in the best position, as I have been informed to have these ballots effectively transmitted to the bases where they can be used, would be the chief paymaster of the Overseas Canadian Expeditionary Force. He is an officer already appointed, .and he would do this work ex-officio, and not because the Government has selected him. Those of us who have been concerned with the introduction of this Bill have been most anxious, so far as possible, to make its operation independent of personal selection by the Government, and the utilization of the machinery of the paymaster's department would operate to make an officer, and not a particular individual, the intermediary through whom these ballots would be forwarded. I know that during this discussion very improbable and far-fetched grounds have been invoked to base suspicion upon, and if we were to designate the Militia Council to be in any way connected with controlling the return of the ballots, it might give rise to the suggestion that in some way or other the Gov-enment would be enabled to control the

selection of particular men. I am anxious to avoid that, so far as I possibly can, and to my mind it might be better not to utilize the officers of any department of Government to return the ballots.
Let it be assumed that whatever machinery we devise here-and we are ready to adopt any well-reasoned suggestions in that respect-may sufficiently secure a genuine vote by the soldier, then it is my belief that once you get that properly sealed into the post office to be transmitted to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, it will be the safest way for the ballots to be returned here. I think that the fewer people through whose hands these ballots are going to pass, the better it will be. Every day we send through the post office things the secrecy of which is most important, and once you get the ballot properly marked and properly deposited in the post office, it is to my mind the best way to secure its not being tampered with in any way. Then, it being addressed to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, when it reaches him here it is in the hands of a responsible officer. It comes to him sealed-and I propose to make that more absolutely clear-and verified, so far as such things can be verified. It is made his duty to put that in a sealed package. He seals it with his own seal, making a package for each electoral district, and he forwards it either by mail or by special messenger to the returning officer; and the returning officer has to produce that in a sealed condition in the presence of the candidates or their representatives. The returning officer puts these ballots in the ballot-box, just as the deputy returning officer puts other people's ballots in the ballot box, and that returning officer will count those ballots. The hon. member for Assiniboia says that all he objects to is the Government counting the ballots. Where he finds in this Bill any provision for the Government counting the ballots, I must say, passes my comprehension. The ballots will be counted by the returning officer. Other ballots are counted by the deputy returning officer. Surely, the returning officer is as much to be trusted as his deputies are. In effect, this is just one more additional deputy returning officer who is the returning officer himself. He will count these ballots at the close of the poll. It was suggested this morning that the provision of the Bill that he shall count these ballots at the close of the poll did not mean, as it does in other Bills, at once after the closing of the poll. We will make that clear. So, the only difference will be that at five
o'clock in the afternoon of polling day, say in the hon. gentleman's constituency, if there be soldiers' yotes, those votes will be counted just as other votes will be counted, in the presence of the candidates or their representatives. Surely, it is impossible to suggest that the Government is going to count the ballots.
So far as those ballots getting back to Canada is concerned, one thing strikes me with regard to the suggestion that they come through the Militia Department or any other department. I would like to avoid even the semblance of these ballots after they are marked being in any way in charge of the Government as a Government. The election is in charge of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. He is not our instrument in any way; his duties are clearly prescribed. As to that part, I think the hon. gentleman should absolve us from the suggestion thai we a?e trying to " count the ballots."

In using'the expression "counts the ballots" I had not in mind the mere fact of ascertaining the number of the ballots for the several candidates after the close of the polls. I was thinking of the whole course of collecting the ballots, forwarding them and counting them,-the whole proceeding from beginning to end.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Will not the hon. gentleman admit that the one thing the Government has to do is to reach a determination as to the man on the other side who shall take the ballots and post them? I do not understand the hon. gentleman to suggest that the Government controls the Post Office; I hardly think he will suggest that. We are trying to meet any difficulty that may be raised by putting this into the hands of a permanent official who must be trusted with everything that has to be done with regard to an election. Let me say further that any other suggestion, short of refusing the soldier his vote, that will tend to prevent the Government from having any control of this operation, I will accept with great pleasure, and I am satisfied that my colleagues will endorse me in that statement.
The hon. member who last spoke (Mr. H. H. McLean) has pointed out that there is no necessary connection between this Bill and an election now or later. He has given a very good and conclusive reason foi that. Might I point out another? We dealt the other day with the Elections Aot. Did anybody come forward and say: Unless you are going to have an election

there is no use of amending the Elections Aot? The bon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) last year, before the war began, moved for a committee-and; we were very glad to assent to that motion- to consider and improve the Elections Act. Did anybody suggest that that hon. member must have come to the conclusion that an election was to he held right off and that otherwise he would not have proposed the amendment of the Act?
There is only one question here-we cannot get away from it; we always come back to it-and that is: should the soldier have a vote, [DOT] and should the machinery for registering that vote be provided? If he should not have a vote, we should not do anything about it now or later. If he should have a vote, now is the time to provide the machinery by which that vote can be registered. What other class in the community would stand for it, if, being entitled to a vote-and I am assuming for the moment that this is admitted in relation to the soldiers-and if the law as it stands did not provide the necessary machinery, they were told: There is not going to be -an election at once; there may be no election, and therefore it is not necessary to do anything? If there lis a right there should be dn the -law means provided for the exercise of that right. As to the suggestion that the Prime Minister should say that there will he no election for a certain length of time, I can hardly see how hon. gentlemen can be serious in such a thing. Is the prerogative of the Crown to dissolve the House df conditions require it to be renounced for a definite period? Yet, that is what hon. gentlemen ane asking foi.
Now, to come back to the objections made to the details of the Bill. If I followed the 'hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff)-and I do not propose to discuss with him past stories of scandal; what we are concerned in, I believe, is how we are going to make this proposed legislation effective-he suggested that a -soldier in barracks in Edmonton, might, under the existing law in that province, and without legislation at all, take dhe necessary oath and register	his	vote. I
quite recognize that that is possible. Before the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) made his suggestion, in considering the matter I had come to the conclusion that there should be added to this Bill a provision that nothing contained in it should prevent the soldier, in a case where he found himself in a position to do so, from exercising his franchise
	(
in the ordinary manner, and, further, that when he found himself in that position, he should so exercise his franchise. This would make it quite clear that this Bill is to apply only to the class of people to whom it is intended to apply, that is, persons who, by reason of their military duties, are prevented from exercising their franchise in the ordinary way. I do not propose to ask that this section be passed at the present time, because I recognize fully the value of the suggestion made by the hon. member for South Renfrew. I want to put the operation of this proposed legislation, so far as it is possible to do so, in a position where even a suggestion of improper control by anybody may be rendered an impossibility. So also do I wish to make this Bill operate to give the soldiers a vote with as little disturbance as possible of the conditions that surround voting generally. If we can find the means whereby the vote of the soldier at home may be taken at polls, or at other places appointed for the taking of such votes where the soldiers are stationed, and the ballots then distributed to the electoral districts where they belong, I shall certainly be very glad to modify the Bill so as to bring about that result. That would reduce the danger pointed out in the method suggested absolutely to the case of men who are overseas. With regard to that, I am glad to have the suggestion for the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens (Mr. H. H. McLean) and I shall be glad to have any suggestion from any member that will provide further precautions with which to surround the giving of that vote, and more particularly that will aim to meet the suggestion that there is any possibility of this Government in any way manipulating or countenancing or conniving at manipulation of the ballots.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My hon. friend, in the course of his observations, stated that the Government could not make any declaration as to the exercise of the prerogative of the Crown with regard to dissolution. I have not uttered a word up to this time upon this subject, nor do I intend to do so. The Government will have to take their own course with regard to dissolution, and, when they dissolve Parliament, whether it he this year or later, the people will be the judge as to whether the reasons for dissolution were or were not sufficient, and whether that course was inspired by patriotic motives, or by motives which were not patriotic. As to the exercise of the piero-

gative of the Crown, and the assertion of my hon. friend that the Government cannot be expected to make any statement on this point, I want to take complete issue with him. It has been done elsewhere: it has been done, more or less formally, in England. The statement has been made, though not formally, that there was no cause for an election; that it would be better to have no election during the war. This statement has been made by ministers and by members more than once in England. But this Government, the Government of Canada, have again and again declared to the people that there is no occasion to exercise the prerogative of dissolution. Not later than last year this was done by the Government. My hon. friend will recall that a statute was passed some years ago by Parliament providing that in the province of Manitoba the election lists shall be prepared every year by a board of judges. The same statute provides also that in the unorganized districts of the province of Ontario a board of judges shall prepare every year, in the months of July and August, the electoral lists. This power is to be exercised mechanically by the board of judges, without an injunction from the Government, but the exercise of that power may be dispensed with by Order in Council passed by the Government. An order was passed last year that there should be no revision of the electoral lists in the unorganized portion of Ontario and in the organized polling districts in the province of Manitoba. The Government last year, therefore, intimated that there would be no election. This being the case, there is no reason to believe that the Government may not be called upon to give an intimation as to whether or not the prerogative of dissolution shall be exercised. I repeat that, whether we have dissolution or whether we do not have dissolution, the action of the Government will have to be judged when the time comes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have a profound respect for any opinion on a question of this kind emanating from the right hon. gentleman, but I entirely fail to see why a provision made by the statute, and the exercise by the Government of the power conferred by that statute, in any way implies that the Crown or any responsible ministers advising the Crown can bind themselves that for a certain period of time, without regard to what conditions may arise within that period of time, they will not perform what those conditions might make 144
it their duty to do. I have already seen, as emanating from the right hon. gentleman, a statement that the fact that the Government exercises the power which it has to exercise some time in the month of June or July, if my memory serves me, whereby it dispenses with the making of the lists for certain districts, binds the Government and the Crown that for a year after that there shall be no dissolution of the House. I must confess that I cannot see any ground for drawing that conclusion. I presume that it would be a fair inference that when a government in the month of June or July, or whatever is the period within which it may do so, does exercise the power of dispensing with the preparing of the lists, it does so because at that time it does not anticipate that there shall be an election. But to conclude from that, that for a year to come the Crown has forfeited its prerogative right to dissolve Parliament and that the ministers have become relieved of what the conditions in the country arising after that action might make it their duty to do in the way of advising the Crown, I must say seems to be an absolute non sequitur. Surely it would be a less deplorable consequence of the exercise of that power that a limited district in the country might, perhaps, find itself without lists than that for a year the Crown's prerogative should remain in abeyance, and that no ministry, no matter how imperative might be the reasons for giving that advice, would be free to advise a dissolution of Parliament. I have great respect for the right hon. gentleman's views, but I certainly cannot concur in that. The right hon. gentleman says it has been done before, but I notice that when he referred to what had been said in England he said "not formally," and that what was said in that country was that there was no occasion for an immediate dissolution and perhaps no cause for dissolution there until after the war. I made no reference to any statement of that kind; I was referring to what I understood to be called for by different gentlemen last evening-an assurance that there would be no election for a certain period of time. I am expressing no opinion whether there ought or ought not to be an election; I only desire to point out that it seems to me that so long as we are going to continue to be governed in accordance with the constitution, no such undertaking can be properly given.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I do not know that I wish to contradict very much of what



my hon. friend has said. I do not contend that the fact that the Governor signs an order to dispense with the necessary formalities for an election is binding upon the Government that there is to be no dissolution; but I say that my hon. friend himself has given the interpretation of that act. It is an expression of the opinion of the Government that there is no cause for an election. Of course, even after the Government have taken such a course as that, occasions may suddenly arise which may compel dissolution, but my hon. friend will agree with me that when the Government dispense with the necessary formalities which must take place before an election, it is a statement to the public that, in the opinion of the Government, there is no cause for a dissolution, and a subsequent dissolution could not be justified unless a new cause compelling a dissolution had arisen which did not then exist. That is the point which I make, and therefore I say that the Government has more than once stated its opinion that there should be no dissolution. It does not follow that there might not be a dissolution if the power of dissolution exists at all times; but it has to be exercised on proper occasions and under proper circumstances. 'All I say to my hon. friend is that when the Government, as they did last year, pass an Order in Council dispensing with the formalities which must take place in Ontario and Manitoba before an election, no dissolution should take place unless there is a cause which did not exist when the order was passed. Something new, something which could not have been foreseen, might cause a dissolution. That is all the Government can undertake. To-day the Government can declare that they see no cause for an election, or that they see cause, or they may say nothing. That is their prerogative and their privilege. I do not ask the Government what they will do; it is their own secret; they may do what they please; but if they dissolve or do not, whatever action they may take, they will have to account for it to the electors; and if they dissolve, they will have to give a sufficient reason to the electors to justify a dissolution.

I can give an instance in point. Last year, when the Legislature of Saskatchewan was called together for what was known as a war session, the programme was laid before the House and the leader of the Opposition in the legislature asked whether, if the Opposition concurred in everything and went in for a short session and brought up none of the subjects

that are usually brought up in an ordinary session, there would be any certainty that there would not be an election before another session of~the legislature was called. The Prime Minister of Saskatchewan promised absolutely that as far as he could see there was no intention whatever of having an election, at least until after there was another session of the legislature.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That only proves that
the Prime Minister of Saskatchewan and I do not agree upon this subject.

It is immaterial to me and perhaps to others when the elections are to be held or whether they are held at all. But it is utterly absurd for any person to suggest, at a time when we are endeavouring to pass a measure to give votes to soldiers who are at the front that there should be no election until after the war is over. This Act contemplates an election during the war.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.
There is no doubt about it. What is the use of the measure if no election is likely to be held.
Hear, hear.

Hon. gentlemen applaud.
I tell them they are wasting their time discussing this measure if there is to be no election and no chance of an election during war time.
Hear, hear.

We do not know how long the war will last, but the Bill cannot be made of any use unless an election takes place during the war. Hon. gentlemen opposite appear to he very much afraid that there will be an election.
Not at all.

I can recall an occa- . sion two years ago when they kept us up here night and day trying to force an election when we were endeavouring to prepare for this war. We endeavoured at that time, as we all remember,. to do our share towards naval participation in the war that we saw coming.
That you saw coining !
Oh, oh.

We were then within a year or two of the previous election, and yet hon. gentlemen opposite were determined to have an election at that time. But they do not want an election now, two years later. The position they take seems to me to be absurd.
Does the hon. gentleman think we should have an election this year?

I am not concerned
whether we have an election this year or not. I said at the start it was immaterial to me when we had an election. The objections that I have heard so far to this measure come from hon. gentlemen who are suspicious that something crooked is going to be done in the taking of votes at the front.
Hear, hear.

I cannot understand the
fury and vehemence of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), backed up by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), who appear to be exceedingly suspicious that something crooked is going to be done in connection with the counting of the ballots. The one thing that these gentlemen ought to suspect most is their own suspicion. There is absolutely nothing whatever in it, and no justification whatever for that suspicion. I would like to know what the Conservative party has done, what this Government has done, to justify any such suspicion. The Conservative party has not conducted a federal election in this country for twenty years. Every federal election in that time 'has been under the control of hon. gentlemen opposite. The hon. gentlemen composing this Government have neveT been guilty of any such actions as would justify hon. gentlemen opposite in suspecting that they were conniving at anything in the way of crookedness in connection with this vote. Not only that, but if we take into consideration the Redistribution Bill passed last year, and the fair and just way in which it was made, I think hon. gentlemen ought to give a little more consideration to the Government. As far as the province of Ontario is concerned, I say the Government waived a great many legitimate' advantages that they could have had from a redistribution.
I do not think that hon. gentleman opposite have any reason to complain about the redistribution, and I do not think they do complain about it. I think it is only right that they should give this Government credit for fairness in regard to redistribution; and the way that redistribution was made should convince them that the election will be conducted fairly and squarely. In the province of Ontario the Conservative party has been in power for ten years, during which time three elections have been held; but not one single charge 144J
of crookedness at elections has been made against the Government; not one protest has gone to trial; there has not been one solitary charge of ballot-switching or crookedness at the polls during all that time.

What about the ten years previous?
Mr! CLARK:	I do not want to refer to
the past. I do not like the suspicions and insinuations of hon. gentlemen opposite against the officers who are to take the vote at the front. I do not see an hon. gentleman opposite whom, if he were an officer, I would not trust with ballots cast in my favour. I do not believe that there is any more justification for suspicion against the officers at the front than there is for suspicion against the gentlemen in the Dominion of Canada who will be appointed returning ofncers and poll clerks. These officers at the front are not only officials of the Government for the purpose of taking the vote, but also officers in His Majesty's service; and I have every confidence that the vote will be taken properly, and I think hon. gentlemen opposite ought to have the same confidence.
I agree with the hon. member for St. John that the question bristles with difficulties; but these difficulties can be surmounted, and the discussion in committee is bound to have that effect. I think all of us will agree that the soldiers should have votes; it is therefore our business to see that they get votes. Proper safeguards must surround the voting so that no crokedness can take place. But I am not apprehensive that there will be any bogus ballot boxes or anything of that sort, and I do not think hon. gentlemen opposite should have any suspicions in that regard. I have the greatest confidence that the officers who will be appointed to take the vote will conduct it properly.

I have not been in the House very much for the last few days, and have not heard much of the discussion. I did, however, hear the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) speak last night. The other day I asked the Minister of Justice if there had been any demand for this Bill from the soldiers themselves. Although I did not think it was a very serious question, the Speaker thought that it was, and ruled it out of order; and the minister did not answer. I understood the hon. member for Calgary to say last night that 12,000 men had enlisted from Gslgary,

and that every one of them had demanded the vote.

I said that 12.000 had enlisted from Alberta. If I said that they had all demanded the vot'e I certainly did not intend so to state. I said that a very large number of the men that I knew had asked that that provision should be made. Of course I do not know the whole 12.000.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I understood him to say that they had all come from Calgary, and had all demanded the vote; and it struck me at the time that that was very different from what had occurred in my section of the country. So far as I can recollect, about 300 men enlisted from the city 'of Woodstock and district. One of the contingents has gone to London, another to Guelph, and the first went abroad. I have met many of these men on the street in Woodstock, but not one of them has suggested that he would like to have a vote; nor have I had any post-cards, letters, or communications of any description from those who have enlisted from Woodstock asking for a vote. I do not say that they would not accept the privilege of voting if they had the opportunity. But I have been wondering where the demand for this Bill came iron). If I were at the front, I think I should be kept busy dodging bullets; I should certainly dodge as many as I could.
I notice that the first section of this Bill provides that the soldiers will have the right to vote for a certain electoral district.
I would like to point out to the minister that a good many of the men who enlisted in Woodstock do not live there. I understand from the papers which give the news of the recruiting that many came from the south riding. I think that a lot of the members of the last contingent enlisted in Tillsonburg or Ingersoll, which are both in the south riding. I know that a number of those who enlisted in Woodstock for the first two contingents are not familiar with our expressions with reference to elections. For instance, a number of these men would . not know the difference between the south riding and the north riding. I am not jealous of these men having votes. I would have no objection whatever, if we could be sure that the votes would be counted exactly as the soldiers wished them to be counted. I am pleased to say that many of the native-born who enlisted from my section of the county are friends of mine anyway. But we all know that most of
IMr. Nesbitt.]
those who enlisted from Western Ontario were natives of the British Isles. They have a perfect right to vote, so far as I know, and I think most of them have been in this country long enough to be entitled to vote and so far as Woodstock is concerned, I think most of those who enlisted would have registered if they had been home at the time of the election. I see that section 1 provides that a volunteer shall be entitled to vote who has been a resident of any place in Canada for a period of not less than thirty days. If my memory serves me right our law requires a residence of three months in a locality.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The provincial law requires a longer period than thirty days.

Somebody has said that
there would be ho necessity for this Bill if it were not the intention of the Government to bring on an election. Whether that be true or not I shall leave to the committee to determine. But, if a number of these men are still in Canada, there is no reason why they should not be voted in the ordinary way. Why should they not be sent back to their own districts? Take districts like Guelph and London; there is no reason why these men should not be sent back to poll their votes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member for
South Eenfrew (Mr. Graham), earlier in the afternoon, made a suggestion looking to provision being made that those who are still in Canada should register their votes in Canada. That would apply to cases where they were near to their own districts. The suggestion was also made that where they were a great distance away we should arrange to take their votes at the places where they may be encamped subject to sending their ballots back to their districts. I do not propose to ask that this particular section be adopted until that suggestion has had the fullest consideration, and I hope we will be able to adopt a system which will substantially meet that view.

I did not hear my hon.
friend from South Eenfrew (Mr. Graham), but in reading the Bill I could not see any reason why something of the kind could not be done. As to the man actually in the fighting line, we know that the people of this country are very strong on sentiment and are very eager to provide everything for the soldier. Now we see that the minister is going to provide votes for them. We have been diligently providing every-

thing that is required to eat or wear and we have been very anxious to contribute in every way possible to their comfort. I cannot conceive that these men either in England or at the front will be worrying themselves about the election if an election comes on. They will have other things to engage their attention if they are really at the front and on the firing line. However, personally, I would have no objection to their voting if it can be done in a feasible way. My hon. friend will readily appreciate that even a person with a non-suspicious mind like I have-rather a stupid one-would not very much like some commanding officer to have the absolute control of how men were to vote either at the front or in Canada. The minister, for whom I have a sincere regard, can quite well appreciate that even people of a non-suspicious mind would not like to be put in that position. We all quite agree with the hon. gentleman who spoke a moment ago that the officers in command of these men are honorable. I know a good many of them who are highly honorable. Still, you know that in politics there is an awful temptation to get the better of the other fellow if you can. There is small blame attached to a person who does that. While I have a high idea of the officers at the front, they would, after all, have the control, practically speaking, of how the men in their regiments were to vote. Nobody would be brutal enough to say to his men that they must vote this way or that way, but they would suggest in some way that would be kindly how the men could vote. You cannot drive a man, but you can coax him very readily. There is a strong objection to having the votes taken in the way proposed. I am not, as I said, of a suspicious turn of mind, but really, is it not asking a good deal from both sides of this House that the officer in charge, whatever his politics may have been before he went to the front, should have the absolute say and control as to how the men under him should vote? That only applies to the men at the front or in England. It strikes me, and I am glad to see that it has struck the minister in the same way, that it would be absolutely unnecessary to provide for voting in that way with respect to the men who remain in Canada. I am glad to see that the minister agrees with the position I take on this matter.
We have all been anxious to close the session and get away home. This session has pot been long in comparison with
ordinary sessions, but there seemed to be a feeling in the air when we first came here that the session would be of a non-partisan character. Sometimes it has drifted down to party discussion. Last night it was very strongly on the border line of straight party discussion. We all came here with the idea that it would be a short session and that we would get home early. When we thought we had everything done this Bill came up. It gives special privileges to a class of the community even if this class is made up of soldiers whom we all honour.
I am glad to see that everybody does the same. I dislike, personally, hot-air loyalty. Hot-air-and-champagne loyalty never did go down with me worth a cent. I dislike to hear it, but I have no doubt that we are all ready to acknowledge our indebtedness to the soldier who has gone to the front to risk his.life. I confess quite freely that I am too big a coward unless I had to do so, but I have a great appreciation of the fellows who do. I endeavour to do my duty as nearly as I can in other ways. We are going to pass a Bill here that gives a special privilege. Is it asked for? If it is not specially asked for, why press it? If it is asked for, let us sit down and work out how the soldier can get a vote if he wants it. If he does not want it why bother with it? What demand has been made? If there has been a demand what kind of a demand has been made?

Mr. Chairman, I
would like to say a word or two with regard to the last remark made by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). He claims that this is a special -privilege that we are giving to a section of our people. I claim that it is not a special privilege, but it is simply giving them the same rights that we who remain at home exercise.

The ordinary registered
voter has to be three months in the locality,_ this provides thirty days. That is the special privilege that I was referring to.

I am glad to have some explanation from the hon. gentleman, because he repeated the remark that it was a special privilege. Thirty days' residence in this country applies only to British subjects. If that is the distinction that he, made, I am glad to learn that that is what he meant.
My hon. friend will also recognize that he and I can only vote where we live.

And we can only vote once, and without this very legislation our Canadian soldiers, who, above all others, have the highest sense of their duty to their country and to the Empire, would be deprived of votes. It is to that I take exception. We have heard during this session talk about frauds being perpetrated on the country, and about injustice having been done to our solders, in the matter of their equipment, and, Sir, that is one important reason why, to my mind, the soldiers on whom these wrongs are alleged to have been perpetrated should have an opportunity of expressing their views. At all events, the fact that the Government has introduced a measure of this kind is evidence that they are not afraid of the votes of the soldiers, and that they believe they have treated them justly and fairly from the very first day they were mobilized in Canada, and since they have been placed side by side with the soldiers of the Empire. We have heard much about the boot scandal, and those of us who saw the men at Valcartier, trudging in the mud and the wet-
I rise to a point of order. I submit that it is not open to my hon. frie.nd to discuss the boot question, which is before a committee of the House.
Oh.
The hon. gentleman opposite will have all the opportunity he wants to discuss the boot question when the report of the committee comes down to-morrow.

The very fact that these investigations have been held is to my mind sufficient justification for extending the franchise to the men who best know all the circumstances. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) and the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) have expressed themselves as being very suspicious that some wrong would be perpetrated if the Government should have supervision over the votes of the soldiers, but has not the Government in office always had supervision over elections, and are they not held responsible in every instance for . the manner in which the elections are conducted? We are doing in this case simply what is done in all other cases with respect to elections. I, most emphatically declare that . if any men are to be deprived of the franchise it should not be the men who go to the front to fight our

battles, and who have the
5 p.m. highest 'Conception of their duties and responsibilities to their native land. There have been appeals from hon. gentlemen on the other side that no election Should be held during the continuance of the war, hut whether we will it or not an election may .become necessary, and it is only in the event of an election taking place when these men are at the front that this measure has been introduced. The obstacles which some hon. gentlemen opposite endeavour to conjure up against this Bill are purely visionary. I wish anything I might say could convince these gentlemen that the officers in command of our troops are honourable and responsible men, and I have enough confidence in them to believe that the vote to be taken at the front will be the purest vote cast in any election throughout the length and breadth of the Empire. I have the most absolute confidence in the men who are facing death in the trenches for our sakes, and I would be ashamed to refuse to place the utmost responsibility in their hands.
The 'hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) has taken exception to the vote being given to men who have been in Canada for a few months only, and he says they cannot understand the issues in an [DOT] election. Let me point out to him that these men will be voting for or against the Government, and not on the individuality of the candidates. I believe in that respect a fairer test of public opinion may be secured than in the ordinary case where two candidates are voted for, one of whom, because of his personality, may command support from the electors which does not represent the feeling of the community on the policy of the party he supports. It is in my opinion more desirable to have a fair test of public opinion on the issues before the people, than it is to have a test of the personal standing in the community of individual candidates, and in that respect I can see many advantages in taking the vote for or against the Government, or for an independent candidate, as the case may be. I did not intend to offer any remarks on this subject nor would I had not the discussion been so prolonged. I could not imagine that there would be a man found in this House who would take any serious objection to giving the franchise to the men who are to-day in arms for the defence of the Empire. I know that from many constituencies a large number of men have gone

to the front, but I am thankful that I have never concerned myself about what their political affiliations may be. I have heard some persons express the opinion that most of the officers are of the Conservative faith, hut I do not agree in that view and I hope it is not so. I do believe that in the appointment of officers there has not been the slightest discrimination made on political grounds. The first intimation I had that war had been declared between Great Britain and Germany was from an officer in my county who called me by telephone and asked me to announce at once to the Minister of Militia that he offered his services to go to the front in any capacity that might be desired, and I assume that he was but one amongst hundreds of the officers of the active militia. I believe, Sir, that there are many Liberal officers at the front who will be called upon to look after the method in which these votes are recorded, and hon. gentlemen opposite need not insinuate that there is going to be such a terrible danger' that Conservative officers only will be placed in charge of this work.

The hon. member for
South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) thinks there has been too much discussion already on this Bill, but fet him remember that as to the very first clause which we have been considering most of the day, the Minister of Justice has admitted that it was presented in such a crude state that it is necessary to allow it to stand for further consideration. The discussion of the Bill has not been in vain. In my opinion, this Bill is bristling with difficulties and every section will have to be considered carefully, so that I apprehend that it will take not only to-day but perhaps several other days to get it into shape, so that the soldiers at the front, the soldiers in Bermuda, and the soldiers mobilized in Canada, can vote properly and have their vote surrounded with such safeguards as to afford that protection which every honest voter desires. The hon. gentleman, therefore, is mistaken in thinking we have taken up too much time in discussing this Bill.
The hon. gentleman misunderstood me; I did not refer to the discussion on the details of the Bill, but to the objections raised by hon. gentlemen opposite to giving soldiers votes.

So far as any objection
to giving soldiers votes is concerned, that was decided when the second reading of the Bill passed, and we are now in committee
endeavouring to provide some workable machinery to carry it out.
I would just call the attention of the Minister of Justice to one possibility under section 2. This section provides that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery shall send to the officer in command of each military base in Canada in which volunteers are serving in the present war, and to the officer in command of the Canadian troops at Bermuda, the necessary ballot papers, affidavits and envelopes. As stated by my hon. friend from Queens and Sunbury (Mr. H. H. McLean), sections 2 and 3 are so closely dovetailed that they must be considered to some extent together. Has this contingency suggested itself to the Minister of Justice? The Clerk of the Crown in Chancery sends these documents to the officer in command of the Canadian troops in Bermuda, let us say, immediately after this House is prorogued-no time is fixed, and these' papers could be sent as soon as printed. We understand that there are twelve hundred Canadian troops there who would have a right to vote under this Act. That officer is supposed to keep these ballots, affidavits and envelopes, in his own possession until the writ for the election is issued. Suppose, as might very easily be the ease-and we must provide as well as we can for all contingencies-the officer in command of the Canadian troops in Bermuda is exchanged. He wants to go to the front, and he is sent to the front while the Canadian troops are left in Bermuda. Suppose he takes these papers with him. There is no direction as to what the officer shall do with these ballots, affidavits and envelopes. Nothing is provided in this Act, and I take it that no command from the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery can affect the officer. He acts voluntarily, and he can use these papers or not, as he sees fit. Suppose a British officer is sent to take command of the Canadian troops in Bermuda, one who knows nothing about this Act. The change is not called to the attention of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. When an election is called, the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery sends this cablegram:	" Writ for election is
issued." But the officer in command who receives that cablegram knows nothing about it; he lias no ballot papers and no knowledge of this law-does not know what has taken place nor what his duties are. There is no authority in this Parliament to impose on him any obligation to do anything with regard to these papers. In that case will the vote of the sold;er#

in Bermuda be taken? This section will have to be changed, it seems to me, to provide for a contingency of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are many contingencies that might be suggested. All these voters might die before the elections.
Does not the minister think that is rather far-fetched?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is almost as farfetched as the suggestion of the hon. member, but not quite. The officer in command, if he is called to England, will cease To be the officer in command. He will have received these papers in his official capacity. No doubt he has other documents in charge in his official capacity. He will receive under another provision of this Bill, copies of this law. I think we can safely assume that he has sufficient intelligence and sufficient honesty-
I am not questioning his honesty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -and sufficient ordinary everyday common sense not to take these papers to England. Equally so I think we can assume that the new officer coming to take over the command will take possession of these documents under the law and will ascertain what his duties are. Moreover, these changes in commanding officers will be known to the department here, and we can assume that if it is necessary to communicate the fact of a change of officers, that communication will be made to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. I must say I am lost in admiration at the ingenuity with which the hon. gentleman discovers things that might happen to defeat this law. There are many things that might happen to defeat the law, but I do think that there is no ground for serious apprehension in relation to the particular difficulties he suggests.
The hon. gentleman must remember that every contingency of that kind is provided for in the Elections Act of Canada.

I desire to ask the minister a question. Section 2 provides for "a sufficient supply of ballot papers in form A." Turing to form A, I find that three places are provided for marking the ballot: first, "I vote for the Government;" second, ''I vote for the Opposition;" third, "I vote for the independent candidate." Is there any special reason, or was any special reason adduced before the committee, why it should read, "I vote for the 
Government.," and, "I vote for the Opposition," instead of, "I vote for the Conservative candidate," "I vote for the Liberal candidate?" Did the hon. gentleman think it was a better lure to say "Government" and a bigger scarecrow to say "Opposition" or was there some other special reason?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Speaking for one member of that committee, I can say he did not think about lures, still less about scarecrows.
We may think anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, the hon. gentleman is absolutely at liberty to attribute to the Government and to myself all sorts of schemes and contrivances which his vivid and powerful imagination may suggest. But, as he asks me the question, I answer absolutely and unqualifiedly that, as I have said, I gave no thought to lures or scarecrows. I never thought that it would make any difference to the intelligent voters for whom the ballots are intended. It evidently makes a difference to the hon. gentleman, but it never occurred to me that to the intelligent voter it would make the slighest difference whether I said "Government" or "Conservative party," "Opposition" or "Liberal party."

The super-intelligence
that framed this Bill might be too high for apprehension of an idea that would strike an ordinary mind. Let me give the Minister of Justice a case in point. In 1911 we had a general election. In the province of Quebec we had deferred elections; one in Chicoutimi and Saguenay. Before September 21 the Government was a Liberal Government, but after September 21 the Liberal party, who had nominated a certain gentleman as a candidate, found that he had slipped through their fingers. I am not personally aware of the fact, but I was told that he had wired the right hon. leader of the Government that he wanted to be on the Opposition side until the new Government was sworn in.	Practically speaking, the
Liberals, although not in power, were running the affairs of the country until October. When the election started there was a Conservative and a Liberal candidate in the field. What about the case where the soldier or absentee voter votes for the Opposition and there is no Liberal candidate in the field? The hon. Minister of Justice may be wdtty or funny in this matter, but I want an answer to my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Tlie hon. member's
question was: did I see a lure in the word "Government" and a scarecrow in the word "Opposition"?

I did not say that; I asked why you provided for the forms "vote for the Government" and "vote for the Opposition." I must be right, because the hon. gentleman flares up at the words "lure" and "scarecrow."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I was a moment ago accused of being witty; now I am accused of flaring up. Which did I do?
Both.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then I can counterbalance the compliment to my wit against the criticism of my flaring up, and thus dispose of both. The hon. gentleman wants to know why it is that we provide for the voting in this way. We all know under the law what the Government is, and we also know what the Opposition is. When we go to the country, the great issue before the people will be whether the Government has been administering the affairs of this country for the last few years in such manner that it is deserving of the continued confidence of the people. Therefore it seemed to me that we were providing, in as effective a way as we could devise, for voting upon the great substantial issue between the parties.
What about the independent candidate? He is not recognized by law.

We conceived that there might be a candidate in some cases who did not claim to support either the Government or the Opposition, and while the law does not deal with such candidate, that is a condition which, I think, should be intelligible to anybody without explanation. I am quite sure that the hon. member for Maisonneuve might have complained that we had forgotten him if we had not provided for an independent candidate. The soldiers, as intelligent men, will know that there may be an independent candidate who does not take sides as 'between Government and Opposition.
How would the minister act in a case such as the one which I have mentioned in regard to the election in Chicoutimi and Saguenay in 1911?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is a provision in the Act that when any difficulty or doubt arises as to who is the candidate entitled to be designated as the Government candidate or who is the candidate entitled to be designated as the Opposition candidate, the matter shall be determined by the leaders of the respective parties.
How would you advise the returning officers to count the votes in a case like tlie one which I have cited?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Government is undoubtedly the Government that goes to the country; that is the way I would decide it.

One of my objections to this Bill is its provision that the voter shall vote for the Government or for the Opposition. At the next general election you may have as candidates, socialists, nationalists, labour men, who are very proud of their respective parties. It has been suggested that it is better to vote for the party than for the man. I take issue with that view; I do not believe'in it. The policy of a Government is liable to change in a very few months. While the soldiers who have gone to the front may have known something albout the policy of the Government when they left, if the policy of the Government changes-as a matter of fact, the policy of the Government has changed since the soldiers left-they	may vote for
what they believe	to	be	the
policy of the Government, but which really is not the policy of the Government. Suppose you have an election in this country and the fiscal policy of the Government has changed very materially. The fiscal policy is everything with the people; it is the fundamental basis of the cost of living. These men may vote for the Government, believing that the Government still adhere to their old policy, whereas if they knew of the change they would vote against the Government. Of course, it would be difficult to have meetings in the trenches, and as to sending literature to the soldiers, I have seen so many kinds of literature that I do not believe in it. As to the soldiers who are in Canada, I ask the minister if he will allow me or anybody else to go among the soldiers and explain what has happened during the last few months, or further back? It is not more than fair that this should be done. It has been stated that if you adopt the principle of this Bill you open the door for discussion among the soldiers. These men are entitled to know before they cast their votes what really is the policy that they are voting for. It may be said that they will be allowed to attend political meetings during

the course of an election, but T am not sure that they would be allowed to attend meetings of that kind. Besides, if the minister attempts to trespass on the rights of the Minister of Militia he will have a hard time. The Minister of Labour knows something about that; he knows what it is to try even to do his duty in respect of labour conditions when the Minister of Militia has something to say in the matter. I suppose, therefore, that the soldiers will be forbidden to attend any such meetings. In case of a general election next summer those men would not know the fiscal policy of the Government. I emphasize that, because I claim that the new fiscal policy of the Government, with the increase of tariff, is far more important than many of the people of Canada imagine. It is the basis of the cost of living, and I will explain this in my neighbourhood to the best of my ability. It makes no difference to me whether soldiers' votes are polled in my constituency. I am not in favour of having men vote for or against the Government, because, as many men on both sides of the House who will acknowledge, the personality of the candidate has a great deal to do with the result of an election. For this reason I think that we should vote not for the Government or the Opposition, but for a representative. We are voting for the man who we believe will best represent our ideas in Parliament. The man has everything to do with it. In effect this Bill says: simply choose anybody, whether he can speak or think makes no difference provided he is a man who belongs to the Government side or the Opposition side. Then if he gets a majority of the vote, under this Bill he is elected. I do not think that is right. I claim that the people in St. A*nne vote for the Minister of Justice they do not vote for his party; they vote for the man, and he knows it; of course he does. Those soldiers who are in Canada should surely have a chance to vote not for the party, but for the candidate. This is very important and it seems to me that we should have a chance to speak to these men before the election. I am not speaking for myself; the Government may bring on an election to-morrow so far as I am concerned; I am ready. I have even got my lists ready; I did not even wait for the Government. Put in 500 soldier votes against me in my division and it will make no difference. I am pretty safe, so far as that is concerned. I claim that we are in duty bound to explain 
the policy under which the country is going to be administered in future years. That is exactly what our soldiers on the other side will not know rnything about. My hon. friend knows that they are not allowed to read the papers every day. Where will they get time to read the papers? The fact is that it may be better for them not to read the papers. They are under discipline and must submit to that discipline. Then, in many - cases the men may consult the commanding officer as to how they should cast their votes; they may ask him if he knows anything about the Government, what has been done, wnether there has been any change in the situation. If a commanding officer is consulted in this way, what will he say?' Will he say: I do not know anything about it? If he says that the soldiers may say: Well, we do not know anything either, and we will not vote. Suppose the Minister of Justice were an officer, with all due respect for him, and he had a certain number of men under his command and some man came to him and said:	Officer, I would like to
know something about this election:	I
have a ballot here and am supposed to cast my vote for or against the Government but I know nothing about it. Then the minister might be tempted. By all means let him tell the man the conditions; but it is possible that if he happened to be either a Liberal or a Conservative he would lean towards that side in his explanations. That is human nature.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Would he not do that
if he were at home?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Is the soldier in the
trenches in any different position as to voting from the man at home? Any man who happens to be a Liberal or a Conservative may say to the voter at home what he thinks about the situation. If an officer in a regiment at home were asked by a soldier what he thought, he might express his political views. Is it any worse for him to do so when he is abroad? Surely it would not be suggested that we ought to stop all conversation on political questions between the officers and their men.

We must bear in mind that the officer will be indirectly a kind of returning officer. He will have the ballots to distribute and so will be indirectly a returning officer. I do not want to deal with that side of the question so much, because I know the difficulty we are up against. I would like to see a change in the provision

respecting those soldiers who will be in the country at the time of an election. It seems to me that they should have the full power to go and vote where they have a right to vote, or that the machinery should be arranged in such a way that they could be made thoroughly familiar with the real conditions and then have a chance to vote for the condidate and not for the Government or the Opposition. Why should we not give a chance for the Socialists, who are numerous in British Columbia, to vote for their own candidates? They should be permitted to vote for their own men. Then if there are Nationalists in Quebec, they should also be given a chance. We have some twenty of them in the House, that is, so-called. Let us give them a chance wherever they are. Such a plan would be more applicable to the real conditions existing in Canada to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know whether
the hon. member was in at the time, but in response to a suggestion of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) I did say that we would consider a suggestion which he made which looked to providing machinery whereby soldiers still in Canada at the time of an election would vote as nearly as possible as they would vote in the ordinary course. It may be possible that they would have to do that voting not in their own district, but the idea was that means should be provided to collect their ballots. As to the opportunities of soldiers of that class to hear discussions, I am quite sure that neither the Minister of Militia nor any of the military authorities would seek to interfere with soldiers attending such meetings as they desired to attend, when they were not on duty. As to the question whether they will have time from their duty to attend meetings, after all, they will be- in the same position as all other employees who have to take time from their occupations to attend meetings. I am anxious that the soldier shall have every opportunity of informing himself like everybody else, and I certainly think that soldiers here in Canada would be as well informed on current events as any other men. As to the soldier on the other side, I think that some hon. gentlemen have an exaggerated idea of the absolute persistency with which he is supposed to be in the trench shooting or being shot at.
I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
From the point of view of his having time to read or get information, I may be quite mistaken, but I am not aware that there is any disposition to prevent information from reaching the soldier. I think hon. gentlemen have quite an exaggerated idea of the depth of ignorance of the soldier on the'other side as to what is going on here in Canada. The soldiers receive letters and, I have no doubt, newspapers and other documents from their friends in Canada, and I am sure that they will be fully informed on events in this country. If any of us were away from Canada under the same circumstances as they are, we would be only too glad and happy to avail ourselves of every source of information in regard to events at home.
I think that the soldiers over there will be fairly well informed as to what is going on lere.

One defect in this Bill, which has already been pointed out by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) and by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville), is that it provides only for a vote for or against the Government or for an Independent; and it gives the leader of the Government and the leader of the Opposition power to elect representatives to this House. It might easily happen that both candidates in a constituency were of the same party. It happened in my. own constituency in 1908; my opponent was a Liberal. Suppose that there are only a few votes difference (between the two candidates, and that there are enough soldiers' votes to decide the election. Then the party leader has power to say which candidate shall be elected; the candidate in that case would be selected, not by the electors, but by the leader of one of the parties. This is not a democratic measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Those soldiers have said that they want to vote for the man who will follow that leader, and that leader determines which is the man who will follow him.

Under the British constitution and under our own, which i3 modelled on the British,, the personal equation has to be taken into consideration. When the candidates ask for the suffrages of the electors, the electors vote for the one in whom they have confidence, and who they think will support one particular party.
