But still they are not sure that he will support that party; for after the candidate is elected he has carte blanche; he is perfectly at liberty to decide which party he will support. The electors, however, have

confidence in him; but under this Bill they would have to trust the party leader.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If it were possible to secure a situation where all the soldiers should actually know who were the candidates, I do not suggest that under those circumstances this measure would be preferable. This method is suggested only because, as regards the men who go overseas at all events, it seemed impossible to devise an arrangement whereby they could have knowledge of who it was that had been nominated, and then send in their votes in time to be counted on election day. When we were considering the matter in the committee, a suggestion was made which, if I had been alone in the committee, would have been acted upon, that we should give the man a fourth alternative; that is to say, that we should put a fourth space giving the soldier the privilege of saying: I vote for So-and-so, leaving a blank space so that the soldier could fill in the name of the man for whom he wanted to vote. If that commends itself to this committee, I should be disposed to do that, because it would give the soldier an opportunity to vote for a particular man; and though, of course, the soldier would be voting without the certainty that the particular man would actually be nominated, at the same time, with regard to a considerable number of electoral districts, he would be fairly safe in his anticipation that that particular man 'was to be a candidate. I shall be glad to get as near as possible in every respect, so far as the soldiers overseas are concerned, to' the conditions that would prevail if they were at home and able to exercise their vote; but the suggestion of voting for or against the Government or for an independent candidate was thought to be the nearest thing that could be done in cases where it was impossible for a man to know who the candidates were. I might say that this method was followed in the New Zealand Act.

When I was speaking some time ago I used the expression that I was willing to let the soldiers vote, but unwilling to let the Government count the vote. That expression has been taken up by other members, and the Minister of Justice has challenged the correctness of the phrase, and suggested that there is no provision in the Bill whereby the Government can count the vote. I wish to take issue with the minister on that point. I ask him who does count the vote if it is not the returning officer, who is an ap-
pointee of the Government? Therefore, the Government does, in fact, count the vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Government counts all the votes.

Yes. But let me point out the difference between the conditions under which the Government, through the returning officer, counts the votes cast under this Bill, and the conditions under which the returning officer counts the votes under ordinary circumstances. In an ordinary election the ballots are marked and put in a ballot box under the active and direct supervision of scrutineers, sworn and bodily present, who watch the proceedings very carefully to see that what is intended by the voter shall be carried out by the deputy returning officer. When the poll is closed in the presence of those scrutineers, the ballot box is opened and the ballots counted in the presence of those same scrutineers; so that the country is not dependent upon the honesty of the deputy returning officer for an accurate count. He is subject to the check of the presence and activity of the scrutineers of the interested parties. But in the case of this Bill the ballots are sent to the returning officer at some time previous to the day of the count, and they are in charge of the returning officer for the intervening period.
I need not enlarge upon the possibilities of what might be done by the returning officer during the period in which those ' ballots are exclusively in his charge without let or hindrance or observation from any other person whatsoever. My hon. friend will say that I am casting an aspersion upon returning officers. Well, Mr. Chairman, we have had experiences of returning officers, and of actions by our Government, that warrant us in being suspicious under those circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: What experiences?

I will come to that presently. If it were proposed to insert in the Dominion Elections Act a provision parallel to this, whereby the ballots which have been cast on election day should be sealed up and remain in the charge of the returning officer without any observation by the scrutineers, would the minister approve of such an amendment? Would he not be ready to admit that we were placing responsibility upon or confidence in the returning officer that we should not place upon or in him? Now what is the difference between the re-

turning officer under ordinary circumstances and the returning officer under the circumstances contemplated by this Bill?
Under our present law is it not the practice for the returning officers to bring in the ballots from distant points- at all events, in Western Canada and Eastern Ontario?

My hon. friend surely knows how the balloting is conducted. The ballots are marked and handed to the deputy returning officer or the poll clerk, in the presence of the scrutineers of the different parties. They are placed in the ballot box in the presence of those scrutineers, and when the polls close the ballot box is emptied and the ballots counted in the presence of those scrutineers, [DOT]and the count is forthwith issued. The process is entirely under the scrutiny of interested parties, and there are no chances as to what shall occur before the ballots are given, at any rate, their first count; whereas, in the case of this ballot, the box remains in the hands of the returning officer from the time he has received it until the poll is closed on polling day.
The ballots are not in *a box?
No, they are not. That is not a proper protection for the people of Canada ih the conduct of an election.
" When are they counted?
When the poll is closed on polling day, the returning officer opens these ballots and counts them.
In the presence of whom?
In the presence, I presume, of the scrutineers.
The same as with other ballots?

I do not know whether that is so or not, 'but that makes no difference to my point. My point is that these ballots have been in the possession, and under the sole responsibility, of the returning officer for an indefinite period, and none of the parties to the election besides himself has any means of preventing these ballots from being tampered with.
Is that not so in the ease of a recount under the present condition?
Yes, but the ballots have already been counted in the presence of the scrutineers before the appeal is taken.
In the case of a recount, while the final count is pending, the ballots are still in the custody of the returning officer, and may be tampered with?

Undoubtedly, but the ballots have be n counted in the presence of the scrutineers, and a certificate has already been issued as to the result of the polling. There is no question as to the actual count, because in such a case there can Be no dispute, but as to the ballots as to which there may be some measure of dispute, all these ballots are counted in the original count by the deputy returning officer before the scrutineers, and if they are not found in the ballot box when the recount takes place it is absolute evidence that the ballot box has been tampered with.

After the soldier votes the ballot must be returned to some individual. Whom would my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) suggest in place of the returning officer? Has my hon. friend any suggestion to make as to the form in which the ballot should be returned, if this proposal is not satisfactory?
I am not making any suggestions. I am replying to the assertion of the minister that the Government does not count the votes, I am pointing out that the Government does count the votes.

My hon. friend takes objection to the Bill as it has been introduced by the minister particularly because in this case the ballot is left in the possession of an individual. In what other way would my hon. friend suggest that it should be taken care of which would give greater security?

I am not making suggestions at this moment, but at the beginning of the consideration of the Bill I did make the suggestion that if it was desired that the soldiers should vote, and that they should vote under ordinary conditions, they could be given their qualification to vote wherever they were on election day.
What about the old country?

I was speaking, of course, only of those in Canada. That is the only way I can see to actually protect the public right as well as the right of the individual soldier. In that way it would be absolutely

protected. There are reasons against that being done which were stated by the minister, and I am not arguing on that point. But I have pointed out to the House a method whereby a soldier in Canada might exercise his franchise just as any other citizen would do, or as he would do if he were not a soldier, and the right of the public in regard to the casting of his ballot is protected.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would like to get clearly just what the method is. Does that mean that a soldier in Halifax should be allowed to go to Vancouver?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then I understand it to mean that on the lines of the suggestion of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) we should provide at the military place where the man is, means by which he can vote in Canada.

In regard to the suggestion made by my hon. friend from South Renfrew, I might point out that there is just that undesirability I have already mentioned, that if a ballot is marked in Halifax to be counted in Vancouver, it must necessarily be sent to Vancouver and be held in the hands of the returning officer without check by any other party for such an indefinite period that there will not in my mind be proper or adequate protection for the sanctity of the ballot.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman any suggestion to make in addition to that?

I did make the suggestion at the beginning of the consideration of the first paragraph that if the soldier were allowed to cast his vote at the place, and in the electoral division, in which he was situated at the actual time of voting, exactly as any other citizen and under the same conditions and safeguards, his right and privilege would be protected and the public right to a proper exercise of the franchise would also be protected. I am not making that suggestion to the minister; I am stating a simple fact. The minister shows reasons why that would not be a good wiay to deal with the question and I appreciate his reasons. My hon! friend from South Renfrew made another suggestion which has in it certainly very many elements of advantage, a number of which advantages the Minister of Justice suggested. But there is still that difficulty that I mentioned and I do not think that it would be proper for me to agree

to the provisions of the Bill unless I drew the attention of the minister to it. I do not wish to argue that point at the moment, but I was merely arguing the point that, as a matter of fact, the Government does, count the votes. That is the point I want to put forward and that is why I say I object to the Bill. I do not object to the soldier voting, but I do object to the Government counting the votes when nobody else has a chance to check the Government or its officers in doing so.
In sections 2 and 3 it was provided that the ballots shall be sent to the commanding officer, and then that they shall be distributed by the commanding officer to some other officer, who shall, as a matter of practice, act as the deputy returning officer. He will hand out the ballot to the soldier and will receive back the ballot and the necessary affidavit. As the section reads, certainly the Government has the authority and the responsibility without let or hindrance of deciding who shall be the deputy returning officer who shall actually hand out these ballots, receive them and forward them in. I do not wish to make suggestions, but I think there was a suggestion made by the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens (Mr. H. H. McLean) that there should be some specific officer who, without the choice of the Government, would automatically be. the man to handle that responsibility. That. I think, would be a very decided improvement, but I am taking the Bill as it is, not as it is going to be improved, and I say that when the Government takes the right to pick out whomever it pleases amongst its officers on the ground to act as deputies it is most essentially taking measures to see that only the right votes come in.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) does not wish to be unfair, and I would like to point this out to him. If he will look at the Bill he will find that, while the proposition may not be an effective proposition in his view, it does not take into the hands of the Government the selection of particular officers. We even exclude the High Commissioner from intervention, so that nobody who is of the Government should figure in this, and we made the secretary of the High Commissioner-an officer whom this Government did not appoint-the man who ex officio would take this thing on himself. We left it in his hands-although it inay not be sufficiently definitely stated in the

Bill-to transmit these 'ballots to the proper officers for distribution, and then we provided that any commissioned officer might do this. I think as drafted the Bill is too indefinite on that point and that it requires to be made precise, but it certainly does not afford grounds for the very serious imputation the hon. gentleman has put upon those who drafted the Bill. I have asked my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) for suggestions as to other and better safeguards, and I am willing to put them in, but he persists in saying that this is a deep-lSid scheme to find a way by which the Government will control the men, when all that I am looking for is a method by which this can be done toy persons acting ex officio and not those whom the Government would pick out. And the hon. gentleman does all this to get to the very remote conclusion that the Government counts the ballots. He seems to think there is something criminal about that. I would like to point out to him that perhaps the Bill does not provide proper machinery to take care of the ballots on their way to be counted, but the Government certainly does not count them any more than it counts all the ballots in all the elections, which are counted by the returning officers; and these ballots are also to be counted by the returning officers. I am satisfied that the hon. gentleman does not want to be unfair, but I hardly think it is fair for him to continue putting the imputations on those who drafted this Bill, of having drafted it with a view of manipulating it in the most absolutely and utterly dishonest way conceivable, and with a view of placing themselves in a position where, if the suggestion of my hon. friend has any foundation, they are supposed to go out and see if they can find among our military officers men capable of every trick and device to destroy the genuineness of these ballots. I hardly think that is a fair line of argument.

There is no member of this House against whom I would be less inclined to make aspersions than the Minister of Justice. I am sorry that what I have said seems to have created on him the impression which he has stated to the House. But we are here on very responsible business; we have very serious duties to perform and while I ivant to eliminate any personal idea from what I have to say, I must take facts as I find them. I do not wish to show any personal animosity.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There was most certainly no intention of any personal animosity on my part.

I know that, and I know that the minister has been very fair and very reasonable in everything he has said, but I must take this view: this is not the Bill of a committee; this is the Bill of the Government of which my hon. friend is the Minister of Justice, and of which Bill he is the responsible father. This Bill was introduced by resolution on the authority of His Royal Highness the Governor-General.
Six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is not convenient to proceed with this Bill this evening, and I therefore move that the committee rise.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
The reason being, that following the usual custom we will take private bills after eight o'clock and then
Estimates, as we want to get through the balance of the Estimates.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

stagedirection
speechtext:

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext: ['When I was Minister of Public Works the necessity for a public building in this town was strongly pressed on me, and after giving it most careful attention, I concluded that the town, because of its population and importance, was much more entitled to a public building than many others which had secured public buildings. That money has been
expended, I suppose?
Yes.

Will the Postmaster General please tell me who is the postmaster at Grande Prairie, what is his salary, from whom is the post office building rented, and what allowance does he receive on account of it?

I have not that information here. I will send it to the hon. gentleman to-morrow.
Post Office, 1913-14-outside service-salaries -further amount required, $372,600.

This money is nearly
all expended. The Estimates were made up in September, 1913, and in consequence no provision was made for the salaries of the current year for those taken on after that date. By reason of the expansion of the service, as I explained on my Main Esti-
[DOT]2296

mates, we were obliged to take on a number of employees,- and this is the amount required to pay them.
Mr. MARCH.:	Would the hon. minister please give particulars?

The new employees
were distributed as follows: railway mail clerks, 100; mail transfer agents, 30; clerks and messengers in superintendents' offices, 17; clerks, messengers and porters in inspectors' offices, 39; clerks, letter carriers, messengers and porters in city post offices, 726.

Are these appointments
all permanent?
Yes.

Has the department still
the system of taking on so-called labourers as temporary employees and afterwards drafting them into the permanent service?
No, we take on temporary clerks.
Can one of these he appointed to the permanent service without examination?
He is appointed for six months as a provisional clerk, after which he passes an examination.	*
Has the minister had time to look into the question I brought to his attention regarding a postal sub-office on Sherbrooke street in Montreal?
The inspector is now making an investigation of the matter, and we are awaiting his report.

I have received letters from a number of those interested, including Lt.-Colonel Baker, who took a great interest in the matter and worked unceasingly on it, calling on postmasters in Montreal and getting numerous petitions asking that some postal convenience of this kind be given to this district. At present, except for the ordinary letter-boxes on the street, there are no postal facilities. Sherbrooke is a main thoroughfare and a very busy one, yet it is without postal facilities. Also I have a letter from a leading citizen of Westmount with regard to the post office at the corner of Victoria avenue and Sherbrooke street. This gentleman, who is a former alderman and a leading citizen of Westmount, and greatly interested in the locality, makes the suggestion that when the department decides to provide better post office accommodation for his locality,

it should place the post office on Sherbrooke street instead of on Victoria avenue, because Victoria avenue is not of such great relative importance as formerly.
We will certainly consider the hon. gentleman's suggestion.

I would suggest to the Postmaster General that in future when he opens a small post office in Montreal, it should not be in a store that is closed three nights a week at six o'clock, and early in the other evenings. I do not want to complain of those already there, but the hon. gentleman knows that very often post offices are placed in drug stores which is a convenience to the public, as these stores are open in the evening. One change was made for which I was very sorry. The Government thought they were taking the post office away from a Liberal. As a matter of fact, the man was a Conservative. It is true, I recommended him, but I did so because his store was the best situated place in the parish for a post office.
I desire to put another question for information. Suppose that a person desires to send a registered letter to a member of the House, is it necessary for him to put on it a two-cent stamp and a five cent stamp for registration?

As to ihe latter question, it is not necessary to put a registration stamp on a letter addressed to a member during the session. As to post offices in stores that are closed in the evening, the hon. gentleman will realize that it is not always possible to find a store conveniently situated for a post office that is open after six olclock. Where possible the department places post offices in drug stores, because they are kept open in the evening. That is the policy of the department. I think that what the hon. gentleman says is correct, and I will try to carry out his suggestion.
They took a post office away from a drug store the proprietor of which happened to be a Conservative.
When?

A couple of years ago; it was not under the administration of the present minister. A requisition bearing many names was sent to the department for the opening of a post office, in a drug store which was on the corner of a street. The post office was opened in a dry goods store, three hundred feet away from the corner.

The reason why I asked as to the sending of a registered letter to a member of the House is that at the very post office to which I referred they compelled a correspondent who was sending a letter, to me to pay two cents for postage and five cents for registration. In answer to my correspondent's question, I said that this was absolutely unnecessary.

1 desire to ask with regard to the sale of stamps on Sunday when, as the minister knows, in Montreal, cigar stores and fruit stores are open. I applied for a stamp at a fruit store and was told that they were not sold on Sunday. Has the department any rule to that effect?
I see no objection to the sale of these stamps by tobacconists and druggists.
What I want to know is whether it is against the law to sell these stamps on Sundays?
No, it is not.
Are the war stamps out yet?
Yes, we are issuing them now.
Are they to be used at once?
Not until the 15th.

At the present time rural mail carriers and stage drivers are paid only once every three months. As a rule their salaries are small, and in many cases they have to discount their cheques, as it were, in order to deal with the storekeeper and the moneylender, and when they receive their cheques they have to pay a considerable amount in the way of interest. I would suggest to the minister that he take into consideration the advisability of paying these men every month.

I am informed by the officers of my department that reports are made by inspectors before the mail carriers are paid; and it would be impossible, with the service that we now have at our disposal, to have reports made and the men paid every month.

I would call the attention of the minister to the fact that no rural mail route has been established in my constituency. A few years ago a route was laid out by the late Postmaster General from New Richmond railway station around to 145
New Richmond and Little Cascapedia. Tenders were called for, but no contract was awarded, because the amount proposed to be charged for the service was too high. This is rather disappointing, as New Richmond is one of the most promising localities in the constituency. Has the minister taken any steps in the matter, in the way of calling for tenders or introducing a service in that district?

I am told that it was impossible to make a contract at a reasonable price for the carrying of the mail. There may be some very special circumstances why this has been the case, and if my hon. friend can give me any information on the subject I shall be glad to look into the matter.

I understand that the
lowest tender was $1,000, and that the department considered that to be too high. Has the department taken no steps since then?

I am informed that
nothing further has been done. The $1,000 was considered by the department to be too high.

I received a letter
from my constituency with reference to a condition that has been created by the establishment of a rural mail delivery in * that district. The minister will remember that I was in communication with him in regard to a rural mail delivery route which was asked for last year, and in respect to which, through some error, the answer was given that this route had not been applied for. In the adjoining district a rural mail route has been laid out from River John through the district of Hodson, returning to the village of River John. It was probably intended to afford facilities to a number of the people who have been getting their mail from Hodson post office through this rural mail delivery route, which is still hung up. With the establishment of the rural mail route from River John to Hodson, the Hodson post office has been closed, and the result is that ten or fifteen people who are not on the rural mail route and who' would be on the proposed route if it were established, are not supplied with facilities for getting their mail and are obliged to go a long distance to the nearest office. I would suggest to the minister that the post office at Hodson be opened until the matter respecting the proposed rural mail delivery route to which I have referred is satisfactorily arranged.

I think that that is a reasonable request, and I will look into it immediately.
Mail service-ordinary land service, including rural mail delivery; further amount required, $365,000.

I would ask the minister to urge on his colleague the Minister of Public Works the desirability of spending the appropriation that has been in the Estimates for the last three or four years, a small matter of $5,000, for the erection of a building at Athabaska Landing which will accommodate the post office and telegraph and land offices, on the ground that the accommodation is urgently necessary for post office purposes.

I hope I may take this as a definite promise.

For some time after the opening of the railway the mail was carried from Vancouver to Prince George by all-rail route via Edmonton. I understand that recently that has been abandoned and the old route by stage from Ashcroft has been adopted. It has been represented to me by the Board of Trade of Edmonton that the change is not in the interest of Prince George or more particularly of Edmonton, that the service by way of Ashcroft is not nearly as efficient or as satisfactory and that the former conditions should be reverted to. It is further represented that whatever is done between Ashcroft and St. George the mail service by way of Edmonton should have the preference.
Patrol of the northern waters of Canada- further amount required, $50,000.
Would the minister explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I explained the matter to the House when my Main Estimates were on. The trouble was that our appropriation last year was not large enough for the pur-

pose, and we require $50,000 more in consequence of the loss of the Karluk. The loss of the Karluk with the supplies carried by her necessitated the purchase of the steamer North Star and a quantity of supplies to complete outfitting. The relief of the party from the Karluk also necessitated certain expenditure not anticipated when the Estimate was made up for the present year. To meet these disbursements it is necessary to obtain a supplementary vote of $50,000.

Would the minister give
some more definite particulars than he gave on a former occasion in regard to the number, character, disposition and purpose of the vessels still in commission under that vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I thought I made a fairly definite statement, but I will give a further statement since August, 1913. In the month of August, 1913, the auxiliary schooner Karluk, carrying about half the members of the expedition and a large quantity of supplies, scientific outfits, etc., was caught in the ice some thirty miles off the Arctic coast of Alaska. The ice conditions that year were extremely bad in the Arctic, and no vessel was able to penetrate as far as Herschel island, the ships being held up to the westward of the boundary line between Alaska and Canada. After the Karluk had been held in the ice for some time it was presumed that she was stationary for the winter, and Mr. Stefansson, with three companions, Messrs. D. Jenness, A. McConnell and B. W. Wilkins, left the ship for exploring and hunting purposes and landed on the Alaskan shore. A heavy storm sprang up, the ice near the shore broke away and the Karluk drifted off and for the rest of the winter was carried by the ice in a westerly direction.
On January 11 the Karluk was crushed in the ice and sank. Every preparation had been made for such an event and the party landed safely on the ice with a full supply of provisions, munitions, fuel, etc., and a comfortable camp was established. At that time the sun was still below the horizon, which made travelling on the ice extremely difficult, and it was decided not to make for land until the return of the sun made travelling easier and safer. Land was visible from the shipwreck camp, which was presumed to be Wrangell island, but which turned out later to be Herald island.

Some members of the party chafed at the enforced inaction and were anxious to make an immediate move. Some of these men left the main party and in two detachments ventured out on the ice in an effort to reach land and safety. The members of these two detachments were never seen afterwards, although parties explored the ice and endeavoured to reach Herald island, a"d there is no doubt that, unfortunately, the eight men comprising these two detachments have perished.
The main party left camp on February 19 and reached Wrangell island on March 12. They brought up a large quantity of the supplies taken from the ship, built a house and camped there for the winter. Captain Bartlett, with one Eskimo and a dog team, left almost immediately for Siberia, which he reached after an arduous and venturesome journey across extremely rough ice with many open leads. After 17 days' travelling on the ice he landed about 50 miles west of North Cape on April 4. He then proceeded along the coast of Siberia and finally reached Emma harbour on May 16. Captain Bartlett's trip was a wonderful performance and is evidence of his courage and determination, and there is no doubt that the survivors of the Karluk owe their lives to his enterprise and endurance in his remarkable trip across the ice and along the coast of Si-, beria.
From Emma harbour Captain Bartlett was taken across Behring strait to St. Michael, Alaska, on the whaling steamer Herman, owned by Messrs. Liebes & Co. of San Francisco. This ship interrupted its trading and whaling venture to carry Captain Bartlett to a port from which he could communicate with the Canadian Government, and the thanks of the Government are due to the owners of the vessel for the kind act performed. Captain Bartlett immediately communicated ' with the Department of Naval Service at Ottawa and arrangements were promptly made for the relief of the marooned party. As a result of these arrangements during the summer of 1914 four ships endeavoured to reach Wrangell island to take off the wrecked men. These ships were the .United States revenue cutter Bear, engaged in the patrol of northern waters, the Russian Government steamer Tayrnur and the ice-breaking steamer Corwin and the trading and hunting .steamer King and Winge. After several attempts had been made by these vessels to reach Wrangell island, the 145}
King and Winge managed to reach the island in September and took off the survivors of the crew of the Karluk and a couple of days later transferred them to the United States revenue cutter Bear, which brought the party to Victoria.
To come back to Mr. Stefansson and his three companions, who landed from the Karluk in September, 1913, this party joined the other members of the expedition under Dr. Anderson who, with their ships, the Alaska and the Mary Sachs, were wintering at Collinson point, Alaska. A programme was then drawn up for the subsequent work of the party. It was arranged that in March, 1914, Mr. Stefansson would undertake an exploring trip on the ice in the Beaufort sea, with the intention of returning within about a month. Mr. Stefansson started on this trip rather late in the year and the ice was beginning to move. He intended proceeding north for a certain time and then returning to his starting point if possible. If, however, ice travel became difficult in that direction, he intended to travel to the east with the intention of reaching Bank's Land in the winter of 1914-15. He left instructions that in the summer of 1914 a vessel should be sent along the shores of Bank's Land to establish depots and erect beacons that would guide him on his return trip in the spring of 1915 if he was unable to reach the mainland before that date. These directions have been carried out. The vessel Mary Sachs, under Mr. Wilkins and Captain Bernard, left Hersohel island in the early part of August and touched at Baillie island on August 19; then headed for Bank's Land to carry out Mr. Stefans-son's instructions. The second party, "under Dr. Anderson, left Herschel island on August 10 and Baillie island August 21, on the vessels Alaska and North Star, and established headquarters on Coronation gulf, where they expected to carry out scientific investigations during the fall of 1914, the following winter, and the summer of 1915. It is expected that the expedition will return in the late fall of 1915 or the following winter.
The loss of the Karluk with the supplies carried by that vessel, necessitated the purchase of another ship, the North Star, and a quantity of supplies, in order to complete the outfit of the party. The relief of the party from the Karluk also entailed certain expense, and to meet these various disbursements it will be necessary to obtain a supplementary vote of $50,000.
When was the last word received from the North Star and the Mary Sachs?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It was some time ago, I do not remember the date exactly.
Would it be after or before the close of winter?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Before.
And no word has been heard since winter set in?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think so. The department is expecting to hear word at any time. I will get the facts and give them to my hon. friend to-morrow.
What is the size and character of the North Star?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It was purchased at
Demarcation point from Mr. Anderson at a cost of $13,000. I have not the tonnage here.
Is it the same kind of boat as the Karluk?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think it is a little larger, but I am judging by the price only. The Karluk cost $10,000, and the North Star $13,000. Other circumstances, of course, may account for the difference in price. Still, the North Star is a substantial vessel.
From what the minister has read, there would seem to be no reason for alarm in regard to the safety of Ste-fansson and the two men with him.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Alarm is felt for the safety of Stefansson, but not for those members of the party who are on the Mary Sachs, the Alaska, or the North Star. The hon. gentleman is probably aware that Captain Bartlett was in Ottawa after his return from the North, and he thinks it possible that Stefansson is safe; in fact, he says he will not be at all surprised if Stefansson is found; but at the same time I think there is reason for apprehension.
According to the programme mentioned by the minister, Stefansson was not expected to return until 1915. Have the preparations been made that he requested?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Everything has been done.
This is a matter of more than ordinary interest. Would the minister be good enough to inform the House upon what information from Captain Bartlett he thinks that Stefansson is possibly lost?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Captain Bartlett's idea, if I remember correctly, was that Stefansson should have reached the mainland at an earlier date. I gathered from Captain Bartlett that it was on that account that he thought there was reason for apprehension for Stefansson's safety.
Have arrangements been made or are they being made to have one or more of the vessels up in the North make an attempt to trace Stefansson during the coming summer?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Instructions have been given to that effect. In addition to that, all vessels that were known to be going up North, whether belonging to the United States or any other country, were asked to be on the look-out for any trace of Stefansson.
Which particular vessel will have charge of this search on behalf of the Canadian Government, and who will be in charge of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Alaska, the Mary Sachs, and the North Star are up there now. I forget the names of the officers who are in charge, but whoever they are they will do all they can.
All three vessels have received instructions to make that search?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
At what time were these instructions sent up North? It is a long road up there.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The instructions have been sent, but I could not say just when.

Another thing I want to ask the minister about is the salmon pond at New Mills. This pond was on the Restigouche on the


broadlands above New Mills, but I am told that the experiment was not as successful as it should have been. Would the minister kindly state the reason of the removal to New Mills?
^lr. HAZEN: My hon. friend moved for the papers, and I am sorry they are not before the House. The change was made, I believe, on the recommendation of the fishery officers of the department. There had been trouble with the pond further up the Restigouche river where it was at Flatlands and it was felt that the work could be more successfully carried on where the pond now is at New Mills. The hon. gentleman is quite right; the first year's experiments at the pond were not an unqualified success. There was some trouble in consequence of the collection of sediment and dirt in the pond that interfered with the health of the salmon. That has all been* overcome and my information is that the results are now most satisfactory. Last year they were fairly satisfactory, a considerable number of salmon fry being obtained in the pond and there is every reason to believe that it will be successful now. Has any understanding
been arrived at with the Government of Quebec in regard to the issue of fishery licenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Correspondence on this
subject is now taking place between the Department of Justice and the Department of the Attorney General of the province of Quebec. I have not seen Mr. Newcombe for several days, but when I last spoke to him an arrangement had not been arrived at although I believe there was reason for hoping that an arrangement would be arrived at soon.
I understand that for the present year the existing condition shall continue and that no licenses will be issued by this department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No such agreement-has
been arrived at that I am aware of.
That was the suggestion made.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We contend that the decision given in the British Columbia case is applicable to the province of Quebec, the decision being that there is a public right of fishery existing in tidal waters and, that

being the case, that the administration of this fishery is in the hands of the Federal government. The government of Quebec contend that Magna Charta, under which this public right is given, does not apply to the province of Quebec, that Quebec does not come within the terms of Magna Charta. We are advised by the Department of Justice that that position is not well taken. However, the Government at Quebec does take the position very strongly that the judgment of the Privy Council does not apply to Quebec and we think it very desirable that there should be a judgment of the Privy Council finally disposing of the matter. We suggested to the authorities at Quebec that we should arrange to have a case stated to the Supreme Court of Canada and to the Privy Council that would absolutely decide whether the regulation of the fisheries shall come under the federal or provincial authorities. That was not accepted by the province of Quebec. There has been some correspondence under which the provincial authorities propose that they should go ahead this year and administer the fishery as they have been doing for a good many years in the past and that we should take steps, by arresting some one for violating the law of fishing without a license for the Dominion to bring the matter to the consideration of the courts again. The last correspondence I saw on the subject shows that the discussion has taken place along that line and I believe that an arrangement may be come to. It may be that my hon. friend has information a little later than I have that an arrangement has been come to.

I am sorry to say that I have not, but I hope that an understanding will be arrived at between the two Governments because it will be unfortunate if the population down there find themselves occupying a position between these two authorities and not knowing which has the jurisdiction. I would like to draw the minister's attention to a peculiar state of affairs in connection with the salmon fishery on the Baie de Chaleur and Gaspe coast. The minister knows the great importance of the salmon fishery in the Baie des Chaleurs in the months of May, June and July. The fish are brought up to Dalhousie and Campbellton and placed in cold storage to be kept until ready for shipment to market. Until last year we had a semi-weekly service which collected this fish along the * Gaspe basin and took it to Dalhousie and Campbellton, there to be put in cold

storage. Last year the semi-weekly service between Montreal and Gaspe was discontinued and we were given a weekly service. This year the people of the coast generally, who found the service so useful to them in shipping to Quebec and Montreal, find that it is now of no use to them for the purpose of exporting their fish in May, June and the beginning of July. The result of the change in this service is that we have thousands and thousands of the most valuable Gaspe salmon, that are fished for all the way to a point below Grand river and along the coast of the county of Gaspe, lying there without means of shipment except by railway. The railway has no cold storage cars and can provide no proper facilities and the result is a great deal of trouble and an immense amount of loss. The last time that the Estimates of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) were up I asked him a question on that point and he told me that he was practically powerless. This company, the Baie de Cbaleur Steamship Company, has a two-years' contract for a weekly service from Montreal to Campbell-ton, and it has turned out to be nothing but a freight service. The boat is very uncertain and the people do not know whether it will pass on Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday. The fishermen cannot afford to allow their fish to remain on the wharf waiting for the boat. Consequently, they have to resort to the railway and great loss has been occasioned. I thought that the minister might perhaps bring pressure to bear upon this company as the result of which they would give a semi-weekly service during May and June. This valuable salmon must be kept in cold storage and placed on the market at as early a period as possible and in the best possible condition if an adequate return is to be made to the fishermen.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I shall be glad indeed to urge the matter on the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Naval Service-to provide a further amount for the removal of obstructions in the Fraser river, B.C., Governor General's warrant, $50,000.
Why was this work made necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The obstruction was formed in the first place in 1913 by the building of the Canadian Northern railway road-bed along the bank of the. river at Hell's gate and vicinity. It completely blocked the ascent of salmon to their spawning beds. In view of the great value of the salmon fisheries, immediately following the discovery of
the blockade in the fall of 1913, work was started in making temporary channels to meet the changing heights of the water, and thus many salmon were enabled to pass up. The Canadian Northern railway was then called upon to restore the river to its original lines during the time of low water in February and March, 1914. This they finally started to do in a rather leisurely manner in February, 1914; but they had hardly got under way when a terrific slide came down from the side of the mountain at Hell's gate, and made conditions very much worse than ever. As it became obvious that only by the exercise of the greatest possible energy could the obstructions be sufficiently removed to enable the ascent of the salmon during the coming season, a conference of engineers on the spot was arranged for. The engineers were the department local engineer in charge of the removal of obstructions in rivers, the engineer of the New Westminster Harbour Commission, and the engineer of the Provincial Department of Public Works. They estimated the cost to be at least $60,000, and Teeommended that the work be placed in the hands of the Pacific Dredging Company, which was best equipped to carry it out. This was done, the company to receive ten per cent of the cost as profits, plus rental for the machinery. The work has proved of much greater magnitude than was anticipated, and has been going on ever since. It is expected that it will be finished in April. By the installation Of a temporary sluice and temporary channels, the fish were passed up this year. Representatives of the Canadian
9 p.m. Northern have been in Ottawa and they have taken the matter up with my department. I understand they admit their liability in connection with the first obstruction, but they claim that the 'second slide was not due to any work of construction on their part. That, of course, will have to be fought out with them.

Has the work been
finished?	.

told that it would come to $60,000, and I had $60,000 placed in the Estimates, but to our surprise we found that was not enough. We think this vote will cover the full amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

What proportion of the cost is the Canadian Northern Company willing to pay ; I understand they are willing to pay for the obstructions caused by their own works?

I promised an hon. gentleman that when my Estimates were before the committee 1 would lay on the table a statement of what liad been done respecting steam trawlers. Though the present vote, does not relate to this subject, perhaps I may be allowed this opportunity to put this statement with regard to steam trawlers on record.
Statement re Steam Trawling.
As steam trawlers from France and the United States, as well as those that operate from Nova Scotia ports, fish on this side of the Atlantic, and as even the inshore boat fishermen usually fish more than three miles from shore, it ds obvious that the only permanently effective way of controlling this fishery is by an international arrangement.
In 1910 it was recommended to His Majesty's Government that a conference of representatives of the countries interested, should ue called, with a view to reaching an arrangement for the entire prohibition of steam trawling on this side of the Atlantic.
In 1911 a reply was given in effect, that His Majesty's Government would find it difficult to support such a conference, but suggested that one might be called to consider the regulation of the fishery along the lines of the North Sea Convention.
While there were many reports of destruction of the gear of ordinary fishermen, interference with their operations and injury of fishing grounds, etc., there was little or no positive information in the premises before the Government. Moreover, while the majority of those engaged in the industry were opposed to trawling, there were those who strongly favoured this method of fishing as an improved one that should be encouraged, and the only one by which a constant supply of fish to meet the demands of an increasing fresh fish business in Canada could be supplied. Hence it was considered best to have the affects of such steam trawling as was being carried on investigated before going into conference. In the spring of 1912 it was arranged with the United States and Newfoundland authorities that during that season such investigations would be carried on independently, the understanding being that, immediately following the completion of such, His Majesty's Government would b ? asked to call a conference.
The investigations in Canada and the United States were carried out under precisely similar instructions to the investigators; but the United States took much longer to complete its investigations than was at first anticipated'. The report of its investigators was submitted omy a short time ago.
It is now feasible to ask His Majesty's Government to invite a conference, which it is proposed to do forthwith.
As, however, the conclusions of such conference could not be reached in time to be made effective this year, and as it seems possible that a considerably larger number of trawlers than heretofore will come to this side this year, it is eminently important that some means he taken to protect the ordinary fishermen.
In recent years there does not appear to have been destruction of the gear of the ordinary fishermen on the banks by trawlers. Therefore, if the inshore fishermen are amply protected, there would not likely he difficulty during the present year.
After careful consideration of the matter, it has been decided to do this by a regulation under tbe Customs Act, whereby the master of any steam trawler will be required, before he is granted a clearance for- the fishing grounds, to give tire customs officer a declaration that he will not fish within at least 12 miles from shore. This will apply to French trawlers operating from Canadian ports, and those that do not, do not fish in the immediate vicinity of our coasts. Failure to comply with this requirement or a breach of the understanding will render the master and the vessel liable to the penalties prescribed for a violation of customs regulations.
As boat fishermen do not operate more than nine or ten miles from shore, this regulation will assure them full protection.
The regulation will apply to all trawlers clearing from a Canadian port on the Atlantic coast. While the United States trawlers do not clear from such ports, their operations so far have not extended beyond the Georges Banks, and there is nothing to indicate that they will during the present year.

That matter was duly considered by the Commissioner of Customs/ the deputy minister and myself, and accordingly an Order in Council was passed along the lines mentioned in the statement which I have just read.

speechtext: I think we could, but we would not accomplish much by doing that. If you do not stop the French trawler, there is not much use in stopping the British trawler.

I understand the minister to say that his department enforced the regulation with respect to the operations of these trawlers within the three-mile limit, and that he had no complaints of any kind within the last year. I may tell the minister that he is not properly informed on that point. It is a fact that steam trawlers operated in the Gulf of St. Lawrence along the coast of the county of Inverness last season and the season before. They have adopted a method by which they can evade the regulations and carry on operations without difficulty. They leave port after dark, and begin their fishing along the coast within the three-mile limit before daylight. The minister says that he is going to enforce the regulation to prevent steam trawlers clearing from ports in Canada from operating within twelve miles of the shore. I wish to point out that the vessels of the protection fleet must exercise greater vigilance than they have exercised in the past if they wish to accomplish anything, not only in enforcing this regulation,

but in enforcing the regulations which at present exist. The fact of the matter is that the existing regulations prohibiting the operation of steam trawlers within the three-mile limit have not been enforced, and the result is that half the fishermen along the coast of Inverness county have abandoned fishing altogether. My hon. friend knows that the equipment which these fishermen require is quite expensive, and they have had such sad experiences in the past in the destruction of gear, nets and trawls that they will not now take any further risks. These trawlers leave Port Hawkesbury or some other point in the Strait of Canso after dark; they drop their gear, pursue their course to the Gulf of St. Lawrence and are outside the three-mile limit before daylight. The information which the minister has with respect to the enforcement of these regulations is not correct. The vessels that he sends down there to enforce the regulations, if they wish to accomplish anything, must pursue a vigilant policy, and not remain tied up in port. The only suggestion made by the fishermen along the coast is that the protection fleet should be on duty at night; this is the only way of discouraging the practice which the steam trawlers have of operating within the three-mile limit. Seven years ago, when first I came to this House, I took occasion to criticise the late Government for their laxity in the matter of enforcing these regulations. I have repeated the same charge since then, and I repeat it again" now. The protection vessels cannot accomplish their purpose if they are not right on the spot before daylight.

The hon. member has made the statement very positively, and I do not wish to question what, he says, but if he is right the officials of my department who make reports to me are wrong. So far as I know, the gentlemen who are in the department, and who are the same gentlemen who have been there for a number of years, are thoroughly competent, and are trying properly to discharge their duties. The statement they make is that practically no fishing was done last year by trawlers within the three-mile limit, and in support of that they refer to the fact that during the last year practically no complaints on that score have reached the department. I do not question the hon. gentleman's statement; he has made it more positively than I ever heard it made before. I will at once call the attention of my officials to his statement, and see what they have to say in (regard
to it. But their reports have been such as to convey an entirely different impression from that which the hon. member's positive statement to-night would convey to the House.

My information comes from the fishermen, and they will be very much surprised to find from to-morrow's Hansard that the minister is so ill-informed, I care not what official gave the information. I took occasion in this House to find fault with the late Government for their failure to enforce the regulations, and I say most emphatically that in this case I have the information from the fishermen. I am not surprised to hear the minister say that he has had no complaints this last year or the year before. The reason for that is that the fishermen are discouraged because their complaints were not heeded in the past in this regard and are abandoning the fishing. They cannot afford to buy gear and have it destroyed before daylight by steam trawlers. The fishermen are at my back in this matter.

This is a question of very great importance all around the coasts of the Maritime Provinces, and if the minister would be kind enough to put the text of the regulations on Hansard it would be very interesting. We would like to see his new regulation.
