I have considered the matter carefully for some time, and it is my view that a committee should be appointed to take up the whole question of printing and distributing reports and parliamentary documents, so that it may be done on a more businesslike basis than is pursued at present. In my judgment, hundreds of thousands of dollars could be saved every year if the printing and distribution of these publications were curtailed. One of the recommendations of the commission to which my hon. friend (Mr. Marcil) has referred was a very good one: it was to the effect that the present system of distributing the blue-books should be done away with. These publications are now carted from the Printing Bureau to the distribution office of the House of Commons, and men are employed
23 v>

to carry them around to the rooms of the members, who often refuse to take them, and they have to be piled up in the corridors. It was recommended that a post office or postal station should be established	in	or close to the	PrintingBureau, from which officers of the Post Office Department could send the publications by mail, as a supply for the House of Commons and Senate, and thus save a lot of unnecessary labour and expense. Copies of these publications could be kept in a small library	or	distribution office	in	theHouse	of	Commons for the	use	ofmembers, of the Senate and House of Commons during the session, and a couple of employees could be placed in charge of them. There are now sent to each member two copies of each report published,	which are duplicated	in	the
Sessional Papers, 24 copies of the Trade and Commerce Monthly Report, two copies of the same, in the Customs reports, and two copies of all other reports. It seems to me that there is a great waste of money in this, and that a good business committee composed of one or two of the deputy heads of departments, together with the King's Printer, the Superintendent of Printing, and a Minister of the Crown, would be able to recommend a cominonsense basis on which this distribution should be made. The present system is unbusinesslike and extravagant, and serves no good purpose. I have been told that some of these publications are not taken out of the post office by parties to whom they are granted, and have to be burned, which of course costs money.
Mr. MARCH,: The House is grateful to Mr. Speaker for the attention he has given to this matter, and while the same complaint existed in my time as Speaker I think it has grown even worse since. The French-speaking mepibers of the House have even greater reason to realize the waste, because when the blue-books are printed in English two copies of each are sent to them, and then a year or two afterwards when the translation is made they get another dose of the editions in French. Some of these are technical books and of no earthly use for any general purpo"e. The recommendation of the commission to which I referred, and the further recommendation of His Honour the Speaker tonight, are worthy of the attention of the Government. I wish to know if the minister has taken any action or intends to take any action in the matter.
[The Speaker.]

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I recently submitted to
the Joint Committee on Printing that we could very well cut off half this waste by distributing in future one copy of these documents to each member instead of two copies as at present. If a member required further copies he could send a post-card to the Printing Bureau and get them in reasonable number. The Joint Committee on Printing recommended my suggestion to the House, and the House concurred in that report yesterday. Several members of the House have informed me that they do not wanit these reports at all, and in that way the waste can be still further lessened. In my judgment, that rule should apply to the distribution of the bound copies of Hansard as well, because I think that one bound copy of Hansard for each member instead of two would be quite sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I have before me
the report of the Department of Public Printing and Stationery, in which the King's Printer makes a suggestion to the same effect as that made by Mr. Speaker.
Miscellaneous printing-further amount required, $50,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: This amount is required to pay for printing done during the year, mainly of departmental reports. It is not possible, under our present system, to estimate in advance what will be the amount spent on this service. Let me give an illustration. By an Order in Council the Department of Agriculture is authorized to print as many copies of its report as it desires. Last year they caused to be printed 80,000 copies of a report of about 900 pages. This year, we have had to print 100,000 copies of a report of 1,500 pages, the report of the Central Experimental Farm. iSo, it is impossible for my department to foresee what will be the amount required during the year. I make this explanation to show how it comes that we are asking for this supplementary vote of $50,000.

There should be some control over the number of books printed, and only as many should be printed as are needed in the public interest, so that there may not be a printing of thousands on thousands of books that are unnecessary.

It seems to me that the charges for printing should be grouped under one head. At present, without very great labour, one cannot ascertain what is

the cost of printing to this country. Every department pays for its own printing?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Not for the annual
report.
But for a great deal of printing they do pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Besides all these other items, we have this amount of $50,000, a further amount required for the printing of the year. The items for printing - should be so arranged that on consulting the Auditor General's Report we could see what printing costs the country. If anything is paid for printing documents for the House of Commons or the Senate, let that appear among the items in its proper place.

I desire to make a suggestion to the minister about printing. When printing of a special nature has to be done it is hardly worth while to call for tenders, because you have to deal with those who supply these specialties. But it would be well that the minister should have a plant for these special kinds of work/ Then, when he has ordinary printing to do, such as any newspaper concern can turn out, let him call for tenders. He will thus get the benefit of market prices and will not be at the mercy of a few who seek to monopolize this class of work.
Mines and geological survey-Mines branch- to provide for the cost of experimental tests of low-grade magnetic iron ores with a view to making pig steel direct therefrom on a commercial basis, $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
A committee of the members of the Geological Survey and the Mines Branch, appointed in September last, to investigate and report on the iron mining industry of Canada, and the metallurgical treatment both local and foreign that might be applicable to Canadian iron ores, recommends that a series of practical tests be made to demonstrate the possibility of making pig-steel direct from selected non-marketable ores, or ores now marketable with difficulty, and suggests that such tests be made at the Moffatt-Irving Electric Furnace, Toronto, as will best demonstrate the possibilities of a convenient method towards developing and utilizing some of the low-grade magnetic deposits of this country on a commercial basis.
The cost of this work is estimated as follows:	a series of experimental furnace
runs for thirty days, $3,000; labour, power, electrode consumption, $1,000; supervision, analyses, providing ore, coke flux, etc., 146
$3,000; unforeseen expenses, $3,000; total,
Where are these lowgrade ores obtained?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: In Ontario and Quebec.
I am told that along the shores of the St. Lawrence immense quantities of these low-grade ores can be obtained.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Experiments will be
made with that ore.

There is a lot of it in
the Timiskaming country.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: When the matter came up last year, one of the parties interested in the ore industry in Ontario came here to ask for a bounty from the Government. Instead of paying a bounty the Government appointed a commission to investigate and report. This commission was composed of officials of the Mines Branch and of the Geological Survey. They made a partial report, advising the department to make experiments or tests by the Moffat-Irving process, and this amount is now asked for to provide for such experiments and tests.

From what part of
Quebec is that ore obtained?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
On the north shore,
opposite Anticosti island.
Large deposits of the best iron ore can be obtained in Rimouski and Temiscouata.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
That ore will be examined by the commission.
Adulteration of food, and the administration of the Act respecting fertilizers, fraudulent marking and commercial feeding stuffs, $51,000.

How is this inspection in the matter of adulteration of foods carried on? I remember when there were officers in every town, and the officer in my own town was engaged in canvassing for my opponent practically eleven months of the year. He really did but little work in the line of inspection; he had charge of the voters' lists for the riding. How many employees has my hon. friend in this business?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: In all, for preventive service and survey of adulteration of foods, about 250. No report of any such condition as my hon. friend has suggested has reached me.
Has there been any increase in the number of inspectors?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No.
How are these men paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: By the year.
What is the average salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: About $600.
Does the minister appoint officers in rural constituencies, or only in towns and cities?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Inspectors are appointed in the cities, and make survey of the food in the various districts. Most of the inspectors live in the cities.
What work is performed by the ordinary inspector in the rural districts of the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: They go around and collect all kinds of samples for analysis and inspection.

From merchants and
farmers?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: From every dealer.

Has the minister had any complaints from milkmen of inspectors stopping milk wagons on windy days, emptying a sample into a package and then sending the package to the department with the result that the milk is reported as dirty?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I am not aware that anything of the kind has come to my department.
Adulteration of food, etc.-proprietary or patent medicines, $1,500.
Are these sent to the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
No, the manufacturer has to apply for a license number and to make a declaration that the medicine does not contain certain harmful ingredients. This is in order to enable the department to follow a patent medicine in case it is found hurtful to public health.
Department of External Affairs-salaries, $27,200 ; contingencies, $9,500.
Sir Joseph Pope is at the head of this department. What are the exact duties of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: He has charge of all diplomatic correspondence and work of that kind. He has naturally had a very busy time during the present year. It is a very busy department.

If the Post Office Department had negotiations in connection with

the postal service between the United States and Canada, would the Postal Department hand their brief to Sir Joseph's department and have him conduct the correspondence?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Not necessarily.
We do that ourselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: For example, when we had the case of shooting in Ontario, Sir Joseph went to Washington and arranged the matter. He arranged a settlement there.

I remember trying to have some correspondence with the Interstate Commerce Commission of the United States as well as with the Imperial Government. We carried on a kind of semiprivate correspondence for some time, but when it became official correspondence between the two Governments we had to hand it over to the Department of External Affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
You are quite right in that.
Office of the Conservation Commission- salaries, $39,500.
Are there any changes in the officials of the Conservation Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
No. The commission is
doing very important work and has been very active and energetic in connection with the surveying and development of the natural resources of the various parts of Canada. I believe that under Mr. White a work very valuable to the Canadian people is being carried on. Mr. White is a very energetic and active man, doing very good service.
Are the recommendations of this commission taken up by Council and followed, or are they merely printed and embalmed.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: As far as I know they are always given effect to.

Usually when this item is up we are given the names of the staff with their salaries and some details of their work. It is really a department of Government carried on in an semi-independent way, but the people are greatly interested in it. I had some correspondence with the commission this year myself. The sum of $39,400 is asked for in a lump without a word of information as to the personnel of staff or the work they are doing. I have

no desire to criticise the commission, but unless we have details of this kind we are not in a position to intelligently vote the amount. I am satisfied that the commission are doing a good work; but we may be asked throughout the country about men on the Conservation Commission and their duties and salaries, and unless we are able to give the information it will be thought that we do not know very much about the management of the country's affairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I will see that a detailed report from the deputy minister is placed on the table to-morrow.

For the last few years the
Conservation Commission have had throughout the country a number of demonstration farms. They get farmers to cultivate portions of their farms under the direction of superintendents employed by the commission. I understand that this year that work has been transferred to the Department of Agriculture. Can the minister tell us whether that is correct? Who paid the expenses heretofore? This amount seems rather small for the work they are doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I understand that some arrangement was arrived at between the Conservation Commission and the Department of Agriculture in order that the work should not be duplicated, but just what it was I do not know.
Miscellaneous-Expenses under the Naturalization Act, $20,000.

I brought up this question of naturalization some two or three weeks ago, particularly with reference to repatriating Canadians, and the Secretary of State said that he would make a statement on the subject, but he would first have to cable for certain information to England.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
We will let the item stand until he comes in.
Miscellaneous-grant towards defraying the preliminary organization expenditure of the Canadian Peace Centenary Association-revote, $10,000..

It was announced that some celebrations were to take place in different localities in connection with the Centenary of Peace. Will they take place this summer?
Mr. RuGERS: Nothing has been settled. I am sure that the one-hundredth anniversary of the establishment of peace between Great Britain and her great American daughter, the United States, is a source 1461
of great satisfaction to us all. This amount is asked for to defray any expenses incidental to the celebration.
Miscellaneous-special allowance to the Chief Justice of the' Supreme Court of Canada, to cover travelling and other expenses in connection with his services while acting as deputy to His Excellency the Governor General, $2,500.

Has the Government
ever seriously considered the question of appointing a regular representative at Washington? I do not mean a British representative, as we now have, but a Canadian one. This matter has been discussed in the House on several occasions, and different views have been expressed. Personally, I am not prepared to express any views, but I should like to know if the Government have seriously considered this matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think that the subject has ever been very much considered, at least by the present Administration. A great many things would have to be taken into account before a proposal of that kind could be carried out. The status of any such Canadian representative in relation to the British Ambassador would involve a great deal of consideration. One of two courses would have to be adopted: one would be to attach the Canadian representative to the British Embassy, and the other would be to have an entirly separate representation. The difficulties which would arise in case either course should be adopted are sufficiently obvious to make it unnecessary for me to dwell upon the subject.
Miscellaneous-grant towards the maintenance of the experiments with reindeer in the Canadian Labrador, under the direction of Dr. W. P. Grenfell, $1,000.

How big a herd of
reindeer have we up there?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I am afraid that is rather a difficult question to answer. The reindeer were introduced into that country by ffiy hon. friend the ex-Minister of the Interior. They have been up there for a number of years, but I am afraid have not prospered very well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have taken a little interest in this subject, and have had the advantage of reading a very interesting monograph thereon, prepared by an officer of the Department of the Interior whose name I cannot recall at the moment. It might be worth while at some later date to lay it on the table of the House for the information of the members. There has

been a good deal of correspondence on the subject, and a good many representations have been made to the Government with regard to it. If I am not mistaken, there are in the northern parts of our western country immense herds of caribou, and one gentleman who has paid a good deal of attention to the subject made what seemed to me a pretty sensible suggestion, that more could be accomplished with the caribou in that region than with the reindeer. He made the further suggestion that if some attention were given to the utilization of these herds a great supply of meat might be derived from that northern country. As far as I can recollect, the suggestion was that if the wild animals which preyed on the caribou could be checked in some effective way an enormous source of meat supply might be opened up in that northern country. I was a good deal impressed by the suggestion, but in the hurry and rush of a great many affairs demanding one's constant attention, particularly during the past year, I have not been able to give to it the consideration that it deserves, or call it to the attention of my colleagues as I wished to do.
Miscellaneous-Grant to the Medical Council of Canada, $15,000.

When this matter came
up some time ago I asked my hon. friend whether the council had made a report to the Government and he promised to make inquiries.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am afraid that I have not been able to ascertain that, but I will endeavour to do so. I did write to the gentleman who is representing the council in the absence of Dr. Roddick to obtain some information as to the disposal of these moneys, and the purposes to which they were applied. I have his letter, though not immediately under my hand, and I think he gave a reasonable explanation of the necessity for some assistance under present conditions. It is hoped that as the system becomes more general, which was inaugurated by the Bill introduced by Dr. Roddick, and as more medical practitioners avail themselves of the opportunities afforded by that Act, the funds of the Council will become very much more selfsustaining than at present. In the meantime, while examinations must continue to be held, although possibly very few people apply to be examined, it does seem necessary that some assistance should be given to the association's work. I think we all agree that the purpose to be served by the

Bill and the work which the association is carrying on are very laudable.

I have been informed that the examination fee has been $100 and that the council holds two examinations a year in different cities. If the Council is to receive a grant of $15,000 I should think that it could reduce the examination fee. and I hope it will. In addition to the fee of $100, the candidates have to undergo considerable expense to attend the examinations. At one time the examination was held at Winnipeg, and the students from the East had to travel to Winnipeg for the purpose of undergoing the examination. If the examination is held in Montreal the candidates from the West have to travel to Montreal. I hope that with the aid of this grant the association will be able to reduce by half the examination fee.
To provide for the salary of a private secretary, A. Hinds, $600, and clerical services to the Hon. J. A. Lougheed, a member of the Cabinet and leader of the Senate, $1,200.
Mr. W. T. WHITE moved that the resolution be amended to read:
To provide for the salary of a private secretary, and clerical services to the Hon. J. A. Lougheed, a member of the Cabinet and leader of the Senate, $1,200.
The effect of the amendment is to strike out the name of the secretary. This may change the destination of the grant. I suppose that in reality it goes to the secretary and not to any individual.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know who the secretary is.
The name is mentioned, but my hon, friend the Minister of Finance moves to strike it out.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
British Columbia-Better Terms Commission, $40,000.
What about this Better Terms Commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There has not
been a great deal of progress made since I last reported to the House on this subject. I think it would have been possible to have done so had it not been for the outbreak of the war, although at first sight there does not seem to be a great deal of relation between the one matter and the other. It was arranged that one commissioner should be appointed by the Federal Government, another by the provincial government, and that the third should be selected by the two so ap-

pointed, or, in default of their agreement, that he should be selected by the Secretary of State for the Colonies. We had some correspondence with the Secretary of State for the Colonies, his intervention having become necessary, and we were asked to indicate the length of time for which the services of the third commissioner would be required, and also some other particulars. We were in communication with the British Government on the subject shortly before the outbreak of the war. It will be perfectly apparent to hon. gentlemen that since the outbreak of the war there would be very great difficulty in securing the services of men who would be very suitable for the discharge of such duties and who would have been available under other conditions. Then some question arose with the government of the province as to the exact scope of the reference, as to which there would not have been any difficulty, I think, except that the subject became more or less submerged in view of the exceedingly pressing questions that have demanded the undivided attention of the members of the Government since the war broke out.

The war has produced a peculiar situation. It has rendered the needs of the province greater and the ability of the Dominion to satisfy them less, but as there is no report from the commission I presume there is no use of discussing the matter now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The commission is not really fully constituted for the reason I have mentioned.
Do I understand that two commissioners have been appointed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
Would the right hon. gentleman have any objection to saying who they are?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Bodwell, K.C., was named by the province and Mr. Lash, K.C., by the-Federal Government.
Liquidation Union Life Assurance Company-additional amount required, including charges of counsel representing the Department of Insurance at prosecution of directors, $6,606.74.
That is all the expense connected with it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the balance.
I presume the matter has been settled satisfactorily to all parties?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is the balance required to pay the liquidation expenses and the fee of counsel representing the Dominion on the prosecution of certain directors of the Union Life Assurance Company. My hon. friend remembers that the Union Life had some 130,000 or 140,000 policy-holders throughout Canada, and its affairs got into a very bad condition. We threw it into liquidation and the court appointed, at our instance, an official of the Insurance Department. now the Superintendent of Insurance, Mr. Finlayson, as liquidator. At my special request as Minister of Finance, the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company assumed all the policies. We felt rather obligated to them for doing so, because they paid about $400,000 more than the business was worth on an actuarial reinsurance basis. The only ground for the Dominion assuming the expenses of the liquidation was the widespread character of the disaster which would have resulted to the 130,000 or 140,000 policyholders throughout the Dominion. The Metropolitan Life was unwilling to pay the expenses of the liquidation. The Government thought that we were justified in saying that we would assume those expenses. They have amounted to about $25,000 or $26,000. This amount of $6,606.74 will complete the payment of the expenses of liquidation.
All the policy-holders are protected?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are all protected; they are all taken care of.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend
from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) renew his question about naturalization, and the Minister of Justice will give him the information?
I asked if there had been any change in the law affecting the naturalization of former Canadians residing in the United States who returned to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does my hon. friend refer to former Canadians who have become naturalized citizens of the United States?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I understand it,
under the law prior to the Naturalization Act of last year there was a special provision for a person re-acquiring British nationality who has abdicated it by naturalization in a foreign country. Under the law as enacted last year I understand that

such person would have to be naturalized now just as though he had always been an alien. The provision which dealt specially with the repatriation of persons who formerly had been British subjects has disappeared under the new Act, and the person now who has lost his British nationality by becoming naturalized in a foreign country must become naturalized as any other alien. I am speaking purely from memory on a question of law, but I think I am correct.
Department of External Affairs-to provide for the salary of one clerk in first division, subdivision B, from October 1, 1914, at $2,800 per annum, $1,400.
Who is the new clerk?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
H. C. Borden, private secretary. The work in the office of the Prime Minister is ordinarily very heavy, but during the past eight months it has been exceptionally so on account of the great number of confidential telegrams and other communications despatched from day to day, and on account also of the very great work which is entailed in coding and deciphering the correspondence, which, in many cases, is of a highly confidenial character. The former secretary, Mr. A. E. Blount, who has discharged these duties, with clerical assistance, during
10 p.m. the first three years of the Administration, was much overworked, and I .have found it necessary almost to station a policeman at the office door to forbid him from attendance when he was seriously indisposed. Finally Mr. Blount was practically on the point of giving up his position and seeking some other work which would be less severe, but I made an arrangement with him to stay, on condition that he would have assistance. I made application in various quarters and I have had a great deal of difficulty in securing a person with the requisite knowledge and experience and qualities for the position, but eventually I succeeded.
Office of the Auditor General-contingencies -temporary clerical assistance-further amount required, $5,000.

Before
passing this item, I deem it my duty to make a few remarks for the benefit of those authorities whom it may concern.
A certain parable in the Gospel states that it is as difficult for a thief to enter the Kingdom of Heaven as for a camel to pass through a needle's eye. I believe the Auditor General has in mind that parable in so far as his employing French Can-
adians in his department is concerned. At the door of his office stands a cerberus who keeps a jealous watch in order to stop any French Canadian from entering. The Civil Service list of 1913 reveals the fact that out of 90 employees in his office, only two French Canadians are to be counted. I should think that if the situation was reversed and the English-speaking employees were in such a minority, the walls of this House would crumble away under the vehemence of the remon-. stances of some of my hon. friends opposite.
I deem it my duty to protest strenuously against the perpetuation of such discrimination against the French Canadians in a department of the public service. I hope the authorities who are at the head of that department will see to it that a stop is put to such a practice. I should not be astonished to be told that those two employees are merely translators or stenographers.
Miscellaneous-investigations under the Inquiries Act-further amount required, $2,500.
Is this in connection with the commission of which the gentleman from Newfoundland was a member?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is merely a general vote; I do not think that it has relation to any particular inquiry.
Is it for inquiries that were made last year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think so.
Miscellaneous-to provide for the expenses of the Acting High Commissioner, London. England, $13,000.
Can the Prime Minister tell us now if he has made up his mind as to who is to be the permanent High Commissioner?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have been so busily occupied ever since that I have hardly been able to give the subject consideration, The office of High Commissioner has been of special service to the Government under the conditions that have prevailed during the past eight months. Of course, the status of Sir George Perley as Acting High Commissioner is different from that which has been enjoyed by any High Commissioner in the past, inasmuch as he not only discharges the duties of that position, but he is a member of the Government as well. I think that I have suggested on previous occasions, both in this House and elsewhere, that some closer form of co-operation as to certain matters
.APRIL 9, 1915
might possibly be found in adopting that as a permanent policy. Nothing that has happened during the period in which Sir George Perley has discharged very efficiently the duties of that office would lead one to the conclusion that it would not be a wise policy. I would not, however, desire to be understood as suggesting or intimating that any absolute and definite conclusion has been reached on that subject. The only thing that can be said in the, meantime is that the experiment, if one can call it an experiment, has proved to be a highly successful one under the conditions which have prevailed during the past year, and that very valuable service has been rendered not only to the Dominion, but, I think, to the Empire as well, by Sir George Perley in London.
Militia and Defence-salaries and wages-further amount required, $14,000.

I should like to call the attention of the Minister of Public Works, who, I think, is looking after this item, .to a memorandum which I have received from British Columbia, and which I should like to read to him in order that he may give the committee some information on the subject. I am informed that in March, 1914, tenders for a supply of coal were called for by the Department of Militia, 1 think in Victoria. The contract was awarded to Messrs. Kirk & Company at $7.10 a ton. There are two other tenders, one at $6.90 and another at $6.75, so that Kirk & Co. s tender was the highest. The lowest tenderer was not awarded the contract, but the coal to be supplied under one of the lower tenders was from the same niine as that which Kirk & Co. were supplying-Thus there can be no question of the quality of the coal. I am informed that at a meeting of coal dealers held in Victoria, Mr. Kirk admitted, in the presence of six others, that he gave a commission to the secretary of the Conservative Association of the city. That is a matter which is worthy of investigation by the Government, as it seems to me that it is very reprehensible. It is not good administration to pass over the lowest tenderer where tenders are called and give the contract to a higher tenderer.	-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: What is the difference?

The lowest tender was $6.75 per ton; the next $.6.90 per ton; and the next $7.10 per ton. The contract was given to Kirk & Co. at $7.10, the highest tender. That is the information which I have, and I would be., glad if the minister
would have the tenders submitted tomorrow. I do not like to trouble him so late in the session, but I received the information only a few days ago. This is the first time since then that any item of Militia Estimates has been under discussion.
Will the hon. gentleman give me the name of the party to whom the payment was said to have been made?
Are Kirk & Co. in Vancouver or in Victoria?
They are in Vancouver. They may be in Victoria too. Many of these firms are in both cities.

My memorandum does not say whether it is in Victoria or Vancouver. I think the letter referred to the fact that information was given to my informant while he was in Victoria. Therefore I would assume it was in Victoria.
I would not like for a moment to have it go on record that that occurred with the secretary of the association in Vancouver.
Is Mr. Price secretary of the association in Vancouver?

No. I want to say most emphatically that, so far as I am concerned, we never allow anything of that type to go on. I have never had any knowledge of a practice of that kind going on in Vancouver. There are four firms in the coal business there-Evans, Coleman Evans, Macdonald & Marpole, Vancouver Coal Co., and Kirk Coal Co. They always tender at exactly the same figure, $7 a ton, on coal for the Government, and the orders are usually divided up among the four firms. The hon. member is aware that the firm of Macdonald & Marpole are strong supporters of his party, so there is no complaint on the ground of political patronage.
It must be very clear that this is Victoria, because Mr. Price is mentioned as secretary of the association.
That is not Vancouver.

I judge that is the case also from another statement, because it says: "If you remember, I gave you all the particulars in reference to this when you were in Victoria." My hon. friend is entirely right in insisting on that course; where tenders are called for it is a matter of obligation on the part of the department to

give the contract to the lowest tenderer, else it is a farce to call for tenders. But, as it has been stated here, the Militia Department, .having called for tenders, instead of giving the contract to the lowest tenderer, gave it to the highest. A very objectionable feature of the case is that it seems to be admitted that the gentleman who got the contract made a contribution to the secretary of the Conservative Association, and people will naturally assume that this was a consideration for his insisting on the contract going to the highest tenderer. That is the inference one would naturally draw. Perhaps the minister would, to-morrow, bring down copies of the tenders with the name of the party to whom the contract was awarded?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I shall be glad to bring to *the attention of the Militia Department to what my hon. friend has stated, and to have placed on the table to-morrow their explanation.	*

Before this vote passes, I want to ask a question of the Prime Minister. Perhaps this is not the proper time to do it, but I am not able to be in the House frequently. What method was adopted in paying Canadian soldiers in England? Were they paid by our own cheques or was the money sent to England and paid there? The reason for asking this is that I have received a letter from a constituent enclosing an original letter written by a soldier to a friend in New Brunswick. This soldier says:
There is a general kick among Canadians in general about pay. They cheat us out of 15 shillings to 18 shillings every month and tell us that it takes that much of every man's pay to pay for the exchange on Canadian money to England. You know and everybody else knows that it don't take that much. Somebody is making quite a fortune out of us fellows.
I shall send the letter to the Prime Minister if he wishes to see it. It is an ordinary letter written to New Brunswick. It was sent me by a gentleman in New Brunswick to find out what it means. I had supposed that the money would be transferred to England and paid there in English money, but evidently some other course has been adopted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did make some inquiry as to the system of payment carried out in regard to men at the front. A Mr. Ward, who had had considerable experience, I believe, as paymaster in the navy and who some years ago was appointed

Assistant Accountant General and Paymaster in the Department of Militia, was sent to Great Britain with the first expeditionary force to act as overseas paymaster with headquarters in London. The Department of Militia places sums to the credit of the High Commissioner's office, requisitions are made upon the High Commissioner's office by the overseas paymaster general and he transmits the sums to the regimental paymaster. I understand there is a paymaster for each regiment. The regimental paymasters attend to the payment of the men.
It would seem then that they would be actually paid in English money.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would understand so.

This letter is dated as
late as March 21. Has the Prime Minister had this question brought to his attention before, or has he received any protest?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No. I have
not had the subject brought to my personal attention before. It may have been brought to the attention of the Minister of Militia, but not to my attention.
I hope the Premier will look into the matter, because if it be true, and I have no doubt at all from the tone of the letter that it is true, there is evidently mismanagement somewhere.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am obliged to my hon. friend for bringing.the matter to my attention. If he will send me the letter I will transmit it at once to the paymaster of the Department of Militia and ask for a statement from him in regard to it.

Before this item is passed I would like to ask the hon. Prime Minister a question. Has he received a letter from the mayor of Montreal in which I requested him to do something to help the " out of works " in that city?
I do not know whether the Hon. Prime Minister has received that letter, but this I can say, it remains without reply to this day. I should very much like to know why.
I have spoken in French because my right hon. friend understands that language. I have had no answer to that letter which, as mayor of Montreal, I wrote to my right hon. friend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I remember receiving it, but, as my hon. friend had pub-

lished it as an open letter, I did not understand that he expected any reply; and for that reason, and without the slightest de-.sire to be discourteous, I did not reply.

I think the least thing
my right hon. friend could have done was to answer. I was rather surprised at not hearing from him, because every letter calls for an answer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not really understand it in that way, because my hon. friend published it as an open letter. It appeared in the papers, I think, before I received it. So I suppose it would be proper for me to regard it in that sense, and not as an ordinary letter written from one gentleman to another, and which of course would demand a reply.

The object of the letter
was to induce the Prime Minister to do something for the unemployed of Montreal.
I am 4G years of age, but this is the first time I have written a letter to a gentleman, especially the Prime Minister of Canada, without getting a reply.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would also
say that this is almost the first time that I ever received a letter which had first been published in the papers of the country.

My letter contained a
suggestion to the Prime Minister to bring . down some legislation to help the unemployed of the city of Montreal, where there are 50,000 men out of work. If I could be here every day I would have brought the matter up in the PIou.se myself.
(Translation.) I would like to mention here, that in my official position as mayor of Montreal, I am the representative of one-seyenth of the entire population of Canada and it seems to me that I am at least entitled to a rejoly from the hon. Prime Minister. ,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I appreciate the importance of any communication from my hon. friend acting in his capacity as Mayor of Montreal. Because I 'did not make a reply to the letter, for the reason already mentioned, I do not wish him to think that I did not give my best consideration to his representations. I have been in communication with the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, and also with my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, for the purpose of endeavouring to provide as far as possible any work for the unemployed in Montreal. I am sure my hon. friend realizes the difficulties of the situation-one which has been experienced not only by
municipalities, cities and provinces, but generally, under the difficult financial conditions which have prevailed since the outbreak of the war.

Another open letter was
sent to the Prime Minister by Commissioner MacDonald, and according to the newspapers it was answered, although perhaps we should not believe all that the newspapers say. This was two or three days afterwards.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend's letter was the first.
Militia and Defence-Gratuities to professors of the Royal Military College on retirement, $15,190.	.
On what grounds are gratuities given to professors retiring?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
This is simply following the usual practice. Professor Butler and one or two others have retired this year.
Special allowance to the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, to cover travelling and other expenses in connection with his services while acting as Deputy to His Excellency the Governor General-Omitted from Main Estimates, $2,500.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is necessary on account of the item in the Main Estimates not being the usual amount that has been granted of late years. I think the amount has bean $5,000.

I have never understood that $5,000 was allowed. I understand that the duties of deputy to His Excellency the Governor General simply mean, attending the opening and closing of Parliament. I think $2,500 is the usual amount, but possibly it may be more.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I will get the
Estimates of last year, and endeavour to look it up.

Let the item pass, and my right hon. friend find out afterwards.
To provide for the salary of a private secretary, and clerical services to the Hon. J. A. Lougheed, a member of the Cabinet and leader of the Senate (payment may be made to a member of the Senate staff notwithstanding the Civil Service Act)-further amount required, $600.
This is in addition?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It seems to be the $600 which is usually allowed to private secretaries in addition to their salary as clerks.

Perhaps before we rise
the Prime Minister would give the explanation he promised in reference to the Northwest Mounted Police?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The amount of $60,000 is explained to me by the Comptroller of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police as follows. It consists of three items: The first item of $40,000 is to provide for the expenses of the Baker lake expedition undertaken to inquire into the murder of Messrs. Radford and Street by Eskimo in 1913. The sending of this expedition was not decided upon until after the Estimates for the current fiscal year had been prepared and passed, and the expenditure, including the purchase of a schooner, amounted to $40,000. I made some explanation in regard to this matter last year. These two men were murdered in the North, and after a good deal of consideration of the subject, and after I had consulted with my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), we decided to adopt this course instead of undertaking to arrest the Eskimo. There was evidence which had come to us from reliable quarters that the men who unfortunately met their fate there had contributed probably to the result by undertaking unusual punishment of some of these Eskimo. I have looked into the report of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police as to the expedition but it does not seem that any report has yet been made; at all events it is not in this year's report.
Then there is an item of $10,000 for transport. Owing to the outbreak of the war and to looking after the alien enemies in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, the item of $50,000 for transport, included in -the current year's Estimates, was found insufficient and a further sum of $10,000 is required to complete this service. There is another item of $10,000 for billeting, subsistence and forage. The price of provisions both where men are billeted and for those living in barracks, has increased considerably owing to the outbreak of the war and the failure of the crops in certain portions of the provinces has caused an increase in the rate of both hay and oats. The sum of $10,000 is required to complete this service. These three items make up the total of $60,000 which is asked.

The Royal Northwest Mounted Police are a body of men who are a credit to this country. It is really beyond the comprehension of strangers to understand how the presence of one member of the Mounted Police force in a locality in the west maintains order. I have been through that western country and where
IMr. Graham.]
great crowds were gathered two mounted police would be enough to maintain order, whereas, in the eastern country, you would require a dozen or more .to do the same work.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
They are all very well
behaved.

_ When the Mounted
Police are present I suppose they are, and no doubt at other times also. The Mounted Police have no superiors in the world.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am very much obliged to my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) for his appreciation, in which I entirely agree. As I stated in an earlier part of the session, the men who were recruited to the number of 500 last summer have proved to be a very fine body of men who, in their training and discipline, have made excellent progress and are well up to the standard of the former force.
Mr. L4FORTUNE:	Mr. Chairman, will
you permit me to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Public Works to an item in the Main Estimates of $15,000 for' the construction of a post office at St. Jacques l'Achigan in my riding? When his Estimates were up I brought this matter to the attention of the hon. Postmaster General, and he was kind enough to refer me to the Minister of Public Works, who, he said, was very kind, obliging and just, with the assurance that I would succeed in securing his assent to the construction of this post office. In 1909, when I was elected for Montcalm, the late member for that riding, Mr. Dugas, now judge of the superior court of the district of Joliet, asked me very earnestly to see to the completion of that building. A vote of $15,000 was passed but to my great surprise that sum was taken away in the following sesion of 1911. I asked to have it replaced in the Estimates, but I had no success. In 1912 I came back and asked the same thing with no success. It was only in 1913 that the then Postmaster General, now a judge of the superior court of Montreal, at my request, replaced the item of $15,000._ Still, there has been no construction. A lot was bought and paid for, the plans were made, everything was ready and I was waiting for the tenders to be called for but no tenders have been called for yet. I would like to appeal to the justice of the Minister of Public Works and to ask him to order the construction of that building. St. Jacques 1'Achigan is a

very large and a very nice place. There are two banks, one college, a tobacco manufactory, and a good population, and it is altogether a very flourishing place. The Administration having decided that this post office should be put up, I think that this Parliament might do me the favour I ask. I do not want the building for myself. I am living in Jacques Cartier near Montreal, and I do not need a post office for my correspondence but I simply ask that the building be erected as a matter of justice to my electors. I hope that the hon. gentleman, who is here to do justice to every one, will see that the building is soon put up. I draw his attention again to it. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works

speechtext:
I might make another remark in justice to the late Minister of Public Works, my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). Everything was ready before the election of 1911 and the tenders were to be called for but there was a difference as to the line between the lot that the Government had purchased and the
neighbouring property. The department was ready to call for tenders, but a dispute arose between the Government and the adjoining proprietor which prevented that. I am thankful to you, Mr. Minister, and having heard of your good disposition I know that you will keep your word, and I will find my post office erected before the general election.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: 1 can assure my hon. friend that he can absolutely depend upon it, that he will probably be in a little better position at the next general election than he was at the last.

When I was Minister of Public Works the necessity for a public building in this town was strongly pressed on me, and after giving it most careful attention, I concluded that the town, because of its population and importance, was much more entitled to a public building than many others which had secured public buildings. I had an appropriation put in the Estimates and I actually purchased the site, but delay was caused by some legal dispute which arose regarding the boundaries of the property. Had it not been for the unfortunate result of the election, that building would have been erected long ago.
Resolutions reported.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House proceeded to consider certain resolutions reported this day from the Committee of Supply.

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext: ['With the unanimous consent of the House.\nResolutions concurred in.']

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not the usual practice to receive a report from the Committee of Supply on the same day as that on which the resolutions have been agreed to in the committee, but it is stated in Bourinot that at the end of a session, when there is urgency, it is occasionally done in the Canadian Parliament, though never in the English Parliament. I think it well to let the House have knowledge of what is being done.
That was my understanding, but the Clerk of the House informed me that it was customary in the Canadian Parliament, near the close of the session, and that it was done last year.

With the unanimous consent of the House.
Resolutions concurred in.

stagedirection
speechtext:
